speechtext:
The petition reads: To the Honourable the House of Commons
in parliament assembled
The petition of the undersigned Canadians and British subjects residing in Yukon Territory humbly sheweth
That parliament is now considering Bill No. 18, which if enacted, will be The Representation Act 1947.
That it is proposed by said legislation to include with Yukon electoral district the district of Mackenzie and the electoral district so created shall elect one member of the House of Commons.
That in the opinion of your petitioners it is not desirable to include the district of Mackenzie with the electoral district of Yukon for the reason that it will create a constituency of the enormous area of over seven hundred thousand square miles in extent, unwieldy and impracticable in every respect.
That Yukon territory and Mackenzie district have nothing in common, no community interest of any sort. They are separated by ranges of high mountains. They have no direct intercommunication and are entirely foreign to each other.
Your petitioners therefore pray that the Mackenzie district be not included in or with the electoral district of Yukon and that the words in section 2 of Bill 18 "including the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories" be struck out; and your petitioners will ever pray.
I have a similar petition from residents of the Yukon, the signatures to date running upwards of 400. I should like to inform the
Inquiries of the Ministry

house through you, Mr. Speaker, that many more similar petitions to the same effect are on their way to Ottawa.

maintopic: REQUEST FOR REESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAMME TO SALVAGE FATS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. HAROLD W. TIMMINS (Parkdale): Mr. Speaker, since soap is in such short supply, and hospitals and housewives are protesting such shortage, and since there is a vast wastage of fats in every household, will not the minister reestablish the organization for the salvage of fats in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: REQUEST FOR REESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAMME TO SALVAGE FATS
speechtext:
On April 15 I made a statement in connection with the alleged shortage of soap. It is true that during the war an organization for the collection of fats from domestic establishments did function under the Department of National War Services. We have in effect in Canada an order, which is not in force in any other country, requiring packing houses to defat carcasses before they are sent to butchers. In that way a very substantial amount of animal fat is obtained.
It was found that the practice of collecting fats from domestic establishments or houses did not produce a great deal of fat. The difficulty is that in large centres adjacent to soap manufacturing plants the collection is feasible, but in smaller places, where it is collected in tins and all kinds of odd receptacles and then turned in to butcher shops, the condition of the fat and the smell after it had been in process of collection for a short time brought forth violent protests from people who were asked to collect it. In the result it accounted for only a fraction of one per cent of the amount of fats we use.
While I am glad the hon. member has brought up the question, I think better results can be accomplished by individual householders conserving as much as possible their use of fat, and I take this opportunity of appealing to housewives to do this. But from the point of view of effecting any substantial increase in the amount of animal fats available for the production of soap, collection would not be worth while.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, April 24, consideration in committee of Bill No. 104, to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor ini council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On P.C. 1609.
Mr. HAROLD W. TIMMINS (Parkdale): Mr. Speaker, P.C. 1609 was enacted' in war time. In the beginning, regulations with respect to construction materials were passed in the interests of the war effort. The government decided to curtail the amount of material which might be used in building construction, as well as the amount of labour which could be made available. In the same way the types of houses and the cubical content were

Emergency Powers
rationed, so to speak, to fit the national war economy. That was the purpose for which these regulations were passed.
During the war we had in Canada a priority system with respect to building materials. It did not work very well, because it was tied in with the regulations in the United States and some of the commodities which it was sought to regulate could not be regulated. As a matter of fact the priorities system broke down and was practically discarded.
The priorities officer who regulates construction materials was appointed in 1942, so as a matter of fact we have had almost five years of experience under this order in council, to know whether it works in the interests of the people of Canada, or not.
At the present time P.C. 1609 is being used for the purpose of channeling building materials under a priorities system to certain special groups of government controlled housing. No provision is made for the control and regulation of construction materials for any other purpose. In opening the debate in respect to P.C. 1609 my purpose is to say to the government, that it must show cause as to why these regulations should be continued.
The minister has told us on many occasions, that there are five groups of government controlled agencies which get priorities on building material. We know those groups to be Wartime Housing Limited, Integrated Housing, Veterans Land Act, Housing Enterprises Limited1, and Emergency Housing. I propose to analyse these various housing groups to show what purpose they serve in the national economy, having regard to the regulation of construction materials.
I have before me a return brought down by the minister in reply to a question of mine in respect of housing in Canada in the year 1946. I had asked how many houses were completed under these several housing groups. I have given these figures before, but for the purpose of this discussion I should like to give them again.
Under Wartime Housing there were completed in Canada 6,816 units; under integrated housing, for the whole of Canada, 566 units; under Veterans Land Act, 2,599 units; under Housing Enterprises, 28 units; and emergency shelters, 1,643. That makes in all 11,652 units. That was the total of all the houses that were completed in Canada in 1946, according to the minister's own figures, by housing agencies with which the government had direct connection.
During that same year, 1946, according to the bureau of statistics, there were created in Canada 59,846 housing units. It is clear there-83166-154
fore that the housing units built through government agencies amounted to only a small part of the over-all housing picture for 1946-about nineteen per cent.
It is evident that so far as building materials and their regulation are concerned the end does not justify the means when only 11,652 housing units were built under the priority system, while 48,000 houses were being constructed by 'builders and private owners who had to compete in the open market and get their materials where they could.
The 566 housing units created under integrated housing is not very much of a showing in a whole year-1946. In the Toronto area only 9 builders out of 450 are building under the integrated housing plan. It seems to be the attitude of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that these are the only builders who are entitled to consideration. In fact the minister himself has said on more than one occasion that if you want to build you should get into one of these government priority groups. Otherwise he is not very much concerned whether you get the materials you need. I will read his statement on that in a moment.
Under the integrated housing plan the intention was that the houses in the first instance should be sold to veterans and at ten per cent below the market price. The builder gets a priority to enable him to get his construction materials, and he is protected by the government in case his house does not sell. I have a clipping here from the last issue of the Financial Post a day or so ago, to the effect that already the integrated housing plan is not working out in the interests of the veterans. I am told that in the city of Toronto a builder is required to advertise the house only once in a newspaper, and then if it is not bought by a veteran within ten days, the builder is allowed to sell it to a civilian. The Financial Post says:
The official Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in recent days has lifted its "veterans' preference" restriction from larger houses (in a few centres of declining demand) under the government's "integrated" construction programme. Under this plan, builders are selling to veterans at 10 to 15 per cent below the general market, in return for supply priorities and a sale guarantee.
_ This, the first official recognition of a break in the market for veterans housing, is considered by many in the building industry as forerunner of possible complete withdrawal of the "veterans' preference" stipulation from "integrated" contracts by next fall.
I presume that that means that this integrated housing plan was first and foremost for the veteran. But apparently the veteran is not taking advantage of the plan and is not in
Emergency Powers

sympathy with it, as it does not meet his ideas in acquiring a house for himself. So the veterans are dropping away from the integrated housing plan, and the government is now telling the builder under that plan that he does not have to sell to the veteran, that he can sell to the civilian. The answer which I received in respect to this particular housing group was to the effect that it was to help the veterans first and foremost, and it seems to me that the department must now consider whether this integrated housing plan is going to succeed in the interests of the veteran, or whether it should be dropped. As I have said, in the Toronto area only nine builders are building under the integrated housing plan, as compared with 450 builders who are building under other plans.
Housing Enterprises Limited is an organization which is being carried forward by the loan companies of Canada. I know from having sat in at some of the earlier meetings some years ago that the loan companies did not go into this plan just because they wanted to. They got a considerable amount of prodding to go into it, and it was good business on the part of the government to see that the loan companies bore their share of the responsibility in respect to constructing housing units in Canada. The price and the rentals of these houses are subject to the control of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. But Housing Enterprises has caught up with the same conditions facing all other housing groups, that cost prices and rents are getting too high to suit the pocketbodk of the veteran.
im satisfied that in the city of Toronto, and more particularly in Montreal, rentals of housing units in this group are going to be beyond the reach of the veteran, and under these circumstances I see no reason why Housing Enterprises should have a priority over the ordinary builder, who as a matter of fact is building most of the houses being built in Canada today. According to a recent departmental statement, some 48,000 houses were built by ordinary private owners in Canada last year.
Furthermore, Housing Enterprises Limited is entitled to a ninety per cent loan, so the company has only ten per cent of an investment in the project. That is a very attractive proposition for a building corporation. In addition they are guaranteed some 2| per cent interest on the capital they put into the venture. That makes it an attractive proposition for a building corporation, and I am sure

that if the same opportunities were offered to the veteran who wishes to have a house built by a private builder the veteran would get a betteh deal all around.
I come now to emergency housing. I said a few moments ago that the emergency shelters built in 1946 numbered 1,643. So far as emergency housing is concerned I am satisfied that the government is doing all it can, and is entitled to do all it can, to help out this emergency situation throughout Canada. As a matter of fact emergency housing is a stopgap; it is only a beginning of things; it is only a hold-over in the meantime until we get better housing. Therefore when 1,643 emergency housing units were constructed in Canada in 1946 it added nothing to the overall picture; it was a temporary expedient.
We all know that building material is in desperately short supply in Canada. Lumber yards are working from hand to mouth to turn out the material. I have been in lumber yards and have seen the president of the company working at a lathe turning out the small bits of material which the builder had to take away to finish up small parts of his houses while the builder waited right there. They are desperately short of material, particularly trim, doors, sash, and all the material that goes into the woodwork of a house. In addition there is a great shortage of nails. Today I intend to refer to the question of nails, because I think we are in for a bad time and I should like the minister to help the people of Canada to solve this problem, which will stifle building in Canada during the next two or three months if we do not do something about it. Gyproc lath, window sash, doors, trim, bathtubs, hardwood flooring and sewer pipe are all in short supply. But the greatest cost of building is the loss of time. It matters not how high the cost of the material or the cost of labour may be; that is not the big factor in the cost of housing at all today. The big factor is the loss of time. A house which used to take four months to build now takes eight months to a year. The loss of time all the way through the picture is what runs up the cost of building in Canada.
From time to time during the session the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has told us something about nails. In answer to a question of the hon. member for Vancouver South on March 4, 1947, the minister said, as reported at page 994 of Hansard:
I have not heard of a shortage of nails in any part of Canada during the past two months.

Emergency Powers
On March 6, having received letters from people in my own constituency, I asked this question, as reported at page 1061 of Hansard:
Is the minister not aware that in the Toronto area the shortage is so acute that the builders cannot complete the houses started in 1946, and will he make a statement in regard to the matter?
As a matter of fact the minister did not make a statement. I was not permitted to have the question answered. Following the asking of the question I did receive from builders in Toronto a large number of telegrams and letters which I offered to show to the minister. I wish to place on Hansard a record of the desperate position in which builders in Toronto find themselves in respect of nails. Having heard the hon. member for Peterborough West and the hon. member for Vancouver South say something about the matter, I am perfectly satisfied that the situation is general throughout Canada and has to be faced. The first telegram I received reads as follows:
Cannot start spring housing programme. Need nails to finish last year's work. Desperate dilemma. Please do something.
I happen to know that builder. He is building in the Etobicoke district. He has land on which to build some thirty houses. He is a progressive builder and is erecting a small type of house. He is stifled in respect of his building in 1947. In fact he has not yet finshed his 1946 houses.
I received a telegram from another builder in the Toronto district which reads:
I am roofing balance of twelve houses started last April with very slow progress owing to shortage of all materials. I intended starting fifteen more last fall but have been unable to do so. Very discouraging. Am I to quit or continue? Approximately 75 per cent of my business has been with veterans.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What was your reply?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I asked the minister for his reply. I offered to show him the telegrams.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He wired to the hon. member; I reply to mine.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have not replied to them. I am expecting that the minister has the matter under control because I have it on good authority that his department has made a survey of the whole situation. They must know what the answer is. I am expecting the minister to give me the answer this afternoon.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Nail the minister down.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The next telegram is from the superintendent of a large building enter-83166-154J
prise which is being carried on in Toronto by no other than Connie Smythe, manager of the Maple Leaf hockey team. It is a big enterprise. The telegram reads:
Fifteen houses, six carpenters, one keg of nails; no sign of more.
Here is another telegram from a builder who says:
Have been to five hardware stores; could only secure five pounds of nails of any description.
Here is another one from a man who builds up in North York. He is a man who in ordinary times would build anywhere from ten to twenty houses. Last year he probably built ten. His telegram reads:
Have been to seven hardware stores today; cannot buy one keg of nails. Job held up.
Another telegram reads:
Jobs absolutely held up for nails. Brought three kegs home from Chicago while attending builders convention; otherwise will have to stop building.
I am not going to go through all these telegrams. They are almost all from men who are building small houses. They are almost all from builders who have been in the business for a number of years and most of whom are building 75 per cent for veterans. They are building small homes which the veterans can buy, but they are not able to make delivery. Here is another:
Have eight houses under construction. Have no nails or plumbing. The situation is serious.
Here is what another builder, a returned man, has to say:
I wanted to start ten in February. All staked ready to go. Cannot buy nails. Project abandoned until situation clarified. Nine out of last thirteen houses built for veterans. Shall we build houses or close up shop?
I have given enough of the telegrams to indicate to the committee that the shortage of nails is desperate. I wish to have you understand, Mr. Chairman, that I am not holding any brief for the private builder in this matter. I do not act for any of these people, though I happen to know a number of them. I am speaking in terms of houses for Canada. Here is a letter I have received from a man who is really heart and soul in the house-building business. He is building a large number of houses in the Toronto area, and he says:
We have found_ it impossible to obtain nails throughout Ontario. We normally employ upwards of one hundred men, and because of the nail shortage, we have found it necessary to stop jobs and lay off valuable men.
Emergency Powers

Here is another from a man and his sons who build a number of houses in the east end of the city:
. . . situation in nails is terrible. It is no worse than other items such as plumbing, heating, lumber and doors. Frankly, building is not worth the headache that you get these days, but we are sticking to our guns in the hope that some day, someone, will do something about it. We seem to be powerless.
I will not read more of these, but I shall be glad to let the minister or his department have the file to look through, if he wishes to satisfy himself that the people are telling a story which is true and which would indicate that building throughout Canada will be stifled if something is not done about nails.
What worries me is the fact that the minister seems to think that if you are not a builder under any one of the five government groups you are not doing essential building. In my view these independent dealers are doing much the better job in building houses in Canada; but the answer which the minister gave to the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) on March 18 last would indicate that if you are not in one of these groups you are not doing essential building. Let me quote what the hon. member for Peterborough West said, together with the minister's reply, at page 1471 of Hansard. The hon. member said that hardware stores, contractors and carpenters in his riding had not been able to get nails, and he said he would like to ask the minister where they could get a few kegs of nails because there were none in the Peterborough district. The minister replied:
The production of nails is high as compared with any previous year. Hon. members are well aware that during the steel strike stocks of nails became exhausted, and, at present all pipe lines have not been filled up. I realize that Peterborough may be pretty well out on the pipe line; nevertheless I can assure my hon. friend that there is no real reason why any builder, for priority construction particularly, should have any trouble in getting nails. If my hon. friend refers to so-called non-essential building which hon. members opposite say should be stopped, then I am not particularly worried about whether nails can be had or not. But for any priority work, or for any essential purpose, nails are now available.
I say to the minister that the ordinary building of houses is essential work, and that there are no nails to be had for these men. Apparently, however, the minister is not too much concerned about whether these people who are outside the priority groups get nails or not.
So far as nails are concerned'-I have said this before-if we are going to continue this order in council, which regulates building
IMr. Timmins.]
materials in Canada, and if we found it necessary, in respect of soil pipe, to give an incentive bonus in order to keep the industry going [DOT]-because after all soil pipe is only a small though necessary part of building-then in the same way some incentive should be given the nail manufacturers so that they can produce a larger quantity of nails, in order that building may be kept going for the year 1947.
The minister was good enough to answer a question of mine with respect to the production of nails. I have given these figures before, but I will give them again. He indicated that there were seven firms who produced nails in Canada, and in 1946 production by the ton was 58,843, while in 1947 the estimate was 70,170 tons. Apparently we are coming to a bottleneck, and I suggest to the minister- I hope he has already done it; perhaps he has-that some incentive should be given to the manufacturers in this industry to see that the production of nails is stepped up. It may be the same in the steel industry as it was in the soil pipe industry, that being unable to produce and make enough money out of nails, the manufacturers have turned to other lines in which more money could be made.
I do not think an increase of 20 per cent in production of nails in 1947 is sufficient to take care of the needs of the country, and I know, from clippings I have from newspapers and from the minister's utterances on the subject, that he too is seized of the necessity for stepping up the production of nails in 1947.
One of the things that I find bothersome in these regulations is the fact that industrial building seems to have stepped! away ahead of house building, in 1946, and is still going ahead. If we are to have regulations controlling construction materials in Canada, and if one of the most desperate needs at the present time in Canada is housing, then we should be doing something about the fact that industrial construction is outstripping the building of dwellings.
I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of January 24, 1947, which reads:
MacLean building reports, which are accepted as authoritative by the construction industry in Canada, indicate that whereas the dollar-volume of residential building in Canada increased in 1946 by only 8-8 per cent over the 1945 figure, business construction soared by 116 per cent, this despite the fact that countless thousands of Canadians, including those who have money to build reasonably-priced homes, are without accommodation. Under these circumstances, whose is the responsibility for controlling non-residential building?

Emergency Powers
I have another clipping from the Globe and Mail in which the minister is quoted as follows:
Resistance in some cities to low-cost housing was cited by reconstruction minister Howe today as one of many handicaps under which the department had been working in its housing programme.
And later on:
Mr. Howe declared the government could not afford not to capitalize on the present enthusiasm in industry for expansion. The objective at the moment was to keep both industrial and housing construction going at the same time.
I agree that it is necessary to keep industrial and house-building construction going at the same time, but I say that the ratio of 8-8 per cent increase in 1946 for residential housing as against an increase of 116 per cent for business construction is away out of line. If we are to have these regulations continued then it is time that the department which has control of the situation through the priorities officer did something about it.
I am not unmindful of the fact that the director of Central Mortgage and Housing is seized of the situation, because he said on March 20 last:
Non-housing construction may be a "restraining influence" on residential building this year, D. B. Mansur, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, declared in his 1946 report, tabled in the Commons today by reconstruction minister Howe.
That brings us back to the crux of the situation, that as a matter of fact the department does realize that industrial construction is out-stripping home building in Canada. The minister speaks of 80,000 houses for 1947. I do not see how Canada will reach 80,000 or anything like that number because, if the government touched only 11,000 housing units in 1946 under the circumstances that obtained, it shall certainly not touch more than 11,000 in 1947.
Now all this business of priorities is governed and controlled by the priorities officer. He has been in the job since June, 1942, and so he should know his job. The fact is, I suggest, that the priorities officer has too many jobs. He is timber controller, steel controller and priorities officer. I am not criticizing him, but I am not so sure that he has a grip of the situation, and I say that for this reason. At a meeting of the National House Builders' Association, held some time ago, one of the officers of the priorities branch had the temerity to tell the National Builders' Association that they need not be worried in the year 1947 about the amount of priorities they would get; as a matter of fact, he said, if
they were building under the integrated group they would get their priorities off the top shelf. And he said, "In order to show you just how we are able to give you priorities off the top shelf I want to tell you that in one month this year"-that was in 1946-"we were able to pass on to integrated housing builders 91 per cent of the total material available of a scarce article". That is hardly playing the game, with 91 per cent of all the material available in Canada going to one small group of builders. This national association of house builders is a small group spread across Canada in various centres. As I said, in Toronto there are probably nine who belong to the association; there are a number of them in Hamilton, and so on across the country. They are building under this integrated housing plan, or a good number of them are, but apparently they are not satisfied because here is what they have to say in an extract from the minutes of a meeting of the National House Builders' Association held in Winnipeg last December:
The priorities officer, Mr. Uren, announced that there probably would be 30,000 priorities for housing in Canada for 1947, and Mr. Mansur stated that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would do its utmost to develop housing under the integrated housing plan.
Present indications are that construction proposed under the integrated housing plan will fall far short of meeting the country's needs. Many builders were so dissatisfied with the priories last year that they hesitated to attempt -any more houses than that built last year and many are very sceptical about the priorities system as a whole.
These are the people who are building under the integrated housing plan; these are the people who are saying that they are skeptical of the ability of the priorities system to keep them going in the year 1947. As a matter of fact I asked a question of the department some little time ago with respect to priorities. It occurred to me, having had something to do with the building industry for a matter of twenty-five years, that if there was a priorities system working in Canada, I might ask the department how these priorities were working out, and how much material was passing under them, and might be able to get some information that would be useful to the house and to the construction industry generally. So on March 6 I asked this question:
How much building material was moved under priorities in 1946, in respect to the following groups:	Wartime Housing Limited, integrated
housing. Veterans' Land Act, and Housing Enterprises Limited, of: lumber, nails, building hardware, roofing, soil pipe, tile, plumbing material-
I need not give the whole group of materials, but this was the answer:
The information desired is not in the possession of the dominion government. Priorities for
Emergency Powers

building materials are issued for government sponsored projects designed to provide primarily homes for veterans and their families. Priorities for building materials are issued to contractors and home owners for selected building material items essential for the completion of government approved projects. In order to assemble the information it would be necessary to survey several thousands of contractors who have made use of 25,788 priorities issued during 1946. Although the survey would take several months its results would be uncertain because of the incompleteness of the records kept by some contractors.
So in the first place apparently the priorities system is unscientific, since proper records are not kept. As I understand it, these priorities certificates are for the minimum requirements of those building particular groups of houses and I suggest to the government that as a matter of fact some of these groups who are getting materials, though of course they have to pay for them, are getting more than their share. There has been a bootleg market in existence. I have heard of many cases of nails being bought on the black market in various districts surrounding the city of Toronto. We all know that nails disappear from warehouses, where, as I suggest, too many nails have been stored for the specific projects. It seems there is a great deal of hoarding going on. I know this because six or seven months ago I had in my office an official of Wartime Housing who told me they were stockpiling then. He said they were not going to get caught in 1947 as they did in 1946, and I do not think that is the proper way to carry on. I see no reason why all other building should be stifled until some of these groups have built up their stocks. This priorities system is unscientific; it does not give us a picture of what is going on in Canada, and apparently that picture is not in the hands of the government.
Then, quoting further from the minutes of the meeting of this association in Winnipeg last December, I find this:
Mr. Mansur said that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was not only willing but anxious to do anything to help build more houses on an orderly basis. He also said that he was making a survey of occupancy in Canada and that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has a fairly good knowledge of the housing needs of Canada. When the survey is finally completed they will have some information along these lines.
That was in December of 1946. Probably that survey has been completed long before this, so now the government should know the needs of this nation for 1947. They must know the great bulk of the building is going to be done by the private builders, but at the moment I am sure I do not know how those private builders are going to get the
['Mr. Timmins.}
material with which to carry on. Some little time ago, as many hon. members know, a group of fruit growers came down here from British Columbia. Some of them were in to see me. I said to one of them, "You people package all your fruit out there, and you must need nails for that packaging. How do you get on for nails?" He replied, "Oh, we have that all arranged. We can get all the nails we want. We get a commitment in respect of nails." I don't know where they get their commitment; perhaps the minister can enlighten me. There is nothing in this order in council with respect to nails for fruit growers. It is a regulation in respect of construction material only. If the return that has been brought down showing the production of nails in 1946, has to do with nails for the furniture industry, for the fruit growers and for many other industries, then of course this picture does not help us very much in respect to nails for the building industry, because it indicates quite clearly that the amounts shown are not at all sufficient to meet the needs of Canadian builders and the Canadian people.
The minister has suggested to me, not only in the house but also in a letter, that builders should be using aluminum nails, which are available in certain quantities. I followed up that suggestion to the best of my ability. I found there were some aluminum nails in Toronto, but they were expensive and the builders felt they were beyond their reach in respect of building. Further than that, however, they found that as the wet lumber began to dry out and shrink, these aluminum nails popped right out. Apparently they do not have the bond or bind they should have, in wet wood. The result is that, having put up a panel of wood with aluminum nails, it was not very long before they were springing out, and of course for this reason they were unsatisfactory. Having regard to the fact that industrial building far outstripped residential housing in 1946, and is going to outstrip it in 1947, if the government intends to continue these construction regulations, something will have to be done to give more direction to the building industry.
I have been reading reports respecting building in Canada, and without making a survey in other cities I have looked into the situation in Toronto. According to the Daily Commercial News of April 22, tenders are being called for a skating and hockey arena in North Toronto, at a cost of $300,000. I do not know that that work is to be undertaken immediately, but whether it be this year or next, I see no reason

Emergency Powers
why permission should be given to build hockey arenas in these days when our people need houses.
As I walk through my own district, out through Sunnyside, I see an expensive and ornamental refreshment booth which has been built recently. A large amount of lumber was required for the building of that place, I suggest that this building was not necessary, having regard to the great demand for houses. There should be some sort of permit system as previously, so that only essential building would be permitted. A directive could be sent out by the minister under his authority, because if he has authority under emergency legislation to pass these construction regulations he has authority to direct the provinces and the municipalities as to the kinds of buildings which shall be constructed. A directive that such and such construction is essential and such and such are non-essential would fit the picture. Commissioners of building in cities and towns, with such a directive before them, could chart their way fairly well in 1947.
While I cannot say which building would be essential and which non-essential, I am sure that if a group of builders across Canada were to meet for two or three days they could frame such a directive. I know perfectly well that a skating rink or hockey arena is not essential. And I do not see any reason why the Toronto Transportation Commission should begin their $800,000 project in 1947-until we have more houses for our people. These are factors which occur to me and which, I am sure, must also occur to the minister.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins), who has just taken his seat. All hon. members welcome the addition to our assembly of a member who is vitally concerned with this problem of housing. It is my opinion that housing is still the number one domestic problem confronting the federal government.
I think it must be agreed that wartime conditions have seriously aggravated housing conditions in most of our metropolitan areas. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is very largely responsible for the dissatisfaction existing in Canada in respect of Canada's housing performance. It was under the minister's direction during the war that Canada established so many new records in the field of shipbuilding and in the construction of tanks, planes and all forms of armament. The leadership given by the minister in Canada's production performance at that time created the impression that when the war was over and materials became available, along with a sufficient supply of man-power, we would have similar leadership in the field of house construction.
The hon. member for Parkdale accurately described the situation which exists in all parts of Canada. People who fought to save their homes are finding that houses are not available. Any man who served in the air force knows that machines such as Catalinas were provided by the Department of Munitions and Supply. These machines cost S250,000, but if one was lost or destroyed and the young man escaped with his life, another was available. Some of the bombs used cost up to 810,000. Young Canadian airmen are now finding it difficult to understand how it was possible to use Canadian money and man-power to produce a bomb costing 810,000, ship it by boat and then drop it on Hamburg or Cologne, when in 1946 and 1947 we are unable to use the same Canadian labour and materials to drop $10,000 houses in Hull or Halifax or Sturgis.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do not forget Regina.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I suppose Regina
requires some too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Not bombs.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We do not need bombs, but we do need houses. If the minister of reconstruction would use the same technique and the same imagination in peace time that

he used in war time, we would have an entirely different picture.
The hon. member for Parkdale made reference to the small percentage of our manpower and materials which were going into residential construction. I should like to quote some statistics from Maclean's building reports for October, 1945, and October, 1946. Residential construction in October, 1946, increased 42 per cent as compared with October, 1945. In the same period business construction increased 180 per cent; industrial construction, 266 per cent, and engineering, 391 per cent. In the first nine months of last year only $32.50 out of every $100 spent on construction went into housing.
Everywhere you go in Canada you find that materials and man-power are being made available for the building of theatres, billiard halls, bowling alleys and such buildings. I am not criticizing the proprietors of these enterprises for wanting to use some of their cash to build a money-making structure, but I am concerned about the minister of reconstruction allowing such a large percentage of our tight materials to be used in non-essential construction. If the minister of reconstruction would1 face the housing problem of Canada and guarantee a housing programme for the building of 100,000 new houses every year for the next ten years, he would capture the imagination of the Canadian people and would assure a market for our lumber manufacturers, our cement producers and those who are turning out the hardware and other things necessary for such buildings. If he took the trade union people into his confidence in connection with such a programme there would be no question at all about the outcome. There is sufficient additional personnel in Canada to undertake such a programme. An analysis was made some time ago to find out whether we had the labour and material available to carry out a programme of 100,000 houses per year, and it was found that we could carry out such a programme and still have left over some 73,000,000 bricks, some 2,000,000 barrels of cement, some two billion feet of lumber, a great deal of glass, and plenty of nails.
I think people in all parts of Canada will agree that the building of 100,000 houses would be a much more useful programme for the minister of reconstruction to promote than the building of new theatres in Ottawa, Vancouver or any place else that you go. I know the minister has given the local authorities the responsibility of deciding what is essential and what is non-essential, but I want to tell him that when a law-abiding citizen asks for a permit to build a store, the local authorities find it very difficult to refuse, because a

Emergency Powers
new store is going to produce tax revenue. They have nothing against the man, and although some members of the council may be in a similar business, they do not like to take a stand that would prevent someone else from going into it. I submit that since the minister gave the local authorities the responsibility of making that decision, the results have convinced most people that the local authorities cannot decide how tight materials are to be used.	,
In the part of Ottawa in which I have been living, two new hardware stores have been built. There were two hardware stores serving that particular community and now we have four where a year ago there were only two. I understand that two returned men are running one of them, and1 I know that most people in the community would like to see the returned men get a break. But, if we have a depression, as most people think we soon will, these young men will probably lose all they have. They will probably be unable to survive the crash.

I am sufficiently
familiar with it to know that two new hardware stores have been built and they have not been able to get supplies of hardware and building materials. No doubt they are able to make a living now when prices are high and people have more money, but when the depression comes those who have not the right type of connection or have not been able to accumulate enough to see them through may lose all their money. Ex-service people who 83166-155
put all their worldly possessions into stores and other new businesses may be the first victims.
I think the minister of reconstruction and his assistants should have the responsibility of deciding what type of construction will be considered as essential, and they should retain this responsibility until greater progress has been made in solving our housing problem. When I was discussing the question of housing a year ago I made a number of suggestions which unfortunately were not taken very seriously by the administration. I suggested that the federal government should formulate an over-all housing plan for Canada, that they should take into their confidence the provincial and municipal authorities and work out such a programme around the table. This has not been done, and the trade recession is coming much closer. You cannot work out a housing formula in six days or six weeks or six months. You require enabling legislation to be passed by the provincial legislatures. You must enlist public opinion at all levels of government. The federal government is open to severe censure for having failed up to April 25, 1947 to call a conference of all authorities on housing in this dominion. Until the federal government gives that lead it is not going to be possible for the city fathers in a city like Toronto to make plans for the future development of the metropolitan area. They have no indication as to how much assistance, if any, they may get from the federal authorities.
The other day I mentioned one of the new booklets put out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation entitled "Sixty-seven homes for Canadians." I was particularly interested in the results of the competition recently sponsored by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I think anyone reading this will feel that it has been a most disappointing performance, and there is a perfectly good explanation. The architect has no incentive to take up the planning of houses for people in the lower income brackets. Until some authority makes the necessary gestures, the architect who might do some planning for people in the lower income brackets will be able to sell his wares elsewhere. In the meantime he is only wasting his time. The government's own statistics indicate that in 1942 twenty per cent of the married men in Canada, exclusive of those in the armed services and in agriculture, had incomes of less than $1,000 a year. Taking into account the fact that the people in this income bracket have to have food and clothing, it will be seen that they cannot afford to pay more than $12 or 816 a month in rent

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They are getting a bit more income now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, but not twice as much, and even if they were getting twice as much they could not go into the market now and rent a very attractive place for $24 or $32 a month. The only people to whom the federal government is giving assistance in housing are those in the top income brackets who can make provision for their own housing. For two-thirds of the people in Canada the present housing legislation is of practically no help. Nothing is being done in the way of slum clearance or to provide subsidized housing so that people who are getting only $1,000 a year and can afford to pay only around $12 a month for rent can have decent living accommodation with running water and electric light.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can my hon. friend answer a question that I have asked before? What is the nature of a man's employment who earns only $1,000 a year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think I have the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A great many people in the textile industry are getting less than $1,000 a year, and caretakers in our city schools, and carpenters-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I checked only the other night the last report of the Department of Labour after the minister had raised this question, and I found that in the textile industry many people are getting less than $1,000 a year. One of our troubles is that our housing programme has been formulated by people who have never had to live on $1,000 a year but are more accustomed to thinking in terms of living on $1,000 a month. A great many people in the towns and villages in my constituency never receive $1,000 a year in cash, such as those clerking in stores or working in restaurants, or carpenters, plumbers, and tinsmiths.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is that so in the province of Saskatchewan, with its minimum wage law?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minimum wage law does not provide employment twelve months in the year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am astonished that you have that situation in Saskatchewan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Many are engaged in seasonal work.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not as bad in Saskatchewan as it is in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The fact remains that two-thirds of our Canadian wage earners are getting less than enough to pay for a house under the Central Mortgage programme, and they cannot afford to pay the rents set out in this new booklet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The rents of the wartime housing units run from $21 to a maximum of $32 a month.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The lowest one given on page 5 of this booklet is $25 a month, which of course includes taxes, insurance, water, maintenance and repairs. That $25 will buy a house on a fifteen-year mortgage with a building value of $2,150, and the maximum loan is $2,020. The minister is experienced in the construction business, and he would be performing a great service for the Canadian people if he would have one of his companies embark on the building of $2,500 houses in Canada in 1947. You cannot build such a house today and comply with the specifications of the National Housing Act, because the costs of plumbing and materials are too high. I have no quarrel with that, but with materials in short supply and building costs what they are you simply cannot build the type of house that is listed here under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The minister will agree that he is not getting houses built this year that will be available for $25 a month.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am offering for sale thousands of houses, the wartime houses-[DOT]

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Built for sale?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, and they can be purchased on the basis of payments of from $21 to $25 per month. My hon. friend knows the rental scale of wartime houses, of which we have built 27,000 and are building 6,000 or 7,000 more. The rental runs from $21 to about $32 a month.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have argued with the minister before on the whole wartime housing programme. In the first place I argued that he was constructing potential slums.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I know you did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
At that time the minister promised that these houses would be demolished within six months after the end of the war. I predicted then that these houses would never be demolished so long as people were living in less desirable houses. I am not saying that these are slum houses now, but

Emergency Powers
they are potential slums and never should have been built as part of a long-term government housing programme. I am not saying that they should be torn down-not at all; but they were not the type of permanent house that the dominion authority should build-houses like peas in a pod, crowded together.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is no wartime house now being built on a lot with less than a fifty-foot frontage. Is that considered crowding in your city of Regina?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I admit that wartime houses are a good deal better than those occupied by a good many Canadian citizens.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How wide should they be spaced so as not to be crowded?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If any hon. member will visit communities where there are wartime houses I think he will agree that you have there a potential slum area.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I will agree with nothing of the sort.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The houses are all of the same colour, and built on the same plan, with their chimneys all in line.	.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is not a description of wartime housing. Has my hon. friend never seen wartime housing?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where did he find the chimneys all in line and the colours all the same?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have seen a number.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Tell us one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is one at Wright-ville which I visited when it. was under construction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We do not build them with the chimneys all in line.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They are a pretty poor looking lot compared with what the minister was able to produce in the way of planes and munitions plants during the war. Apparently wartime housing is a permanent housing programme, and a great many of these houses will be here as long as the minister lives.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was told only about two months ago by the top officers of the Legion that the only satisfactory housing being built for the veterans in Canada was wartime housing, and that the hope of the veterans depended on wartime housing. That is the other side of the picture. You might as well have both sides.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If wartime houses are the best that Canada can build for the veterans of world war II, they are pretty cheap looking compared with the planes and munitions plants which the minister constructed during the war, when he built in an imaginative way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to have a view of my hon. friend's own town when he says that these houses are cheap looking. Compared with what are they cheap looking?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I hope the people of Canada are not always going to live in wartime housing. I was born in a log house and I do not apologize for it. But as soon as my father could afford it he wanted a better house for his children. A great many of my people lived in log houses. A great many of the ex-servicemen came from log houses, but they do not want to go back to them if they can avoid doing so. The housing programme of 1947 must be better than that which the minister has visualized in his wartime housing programmn
I am not going to enter into a discussion regarding the merits of wartime houses versus the veterans housing programme. The veteran* are being compelled to pay outrageous prices for the property they will have, but it is a matter of getting a house and they have to pay what is demanded. The fact is that at the present time the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is failing to give leadership which will result in a housing programme being worked out to make use of the raw materials we have in this country and which will ensure employment for the workers in the building industry over the next five or ten years. It is true that more houses were built last year than were built ten years ago, but the houses that are being built do not take into account the needs of the people or the population. I find that in the Toronto area, for example, around Forest Hill 116 permits were issued last year for houses having a total value of $2 million, or an average of 818,035 each. There are not many veterans who can take advantage of a house costing $18,000. One of my^ quarrels with this type of housing in this period when we are so short of many materials is that there are two or three bathtubs going into these luxury houses. If the minister had acted on the advice I gave last year he would have continued the responsibility he had of deciding what was essential housing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend can tell me what is essential housing. He complains about wartime housing being too cheap
Emergency Powers

and of substandard construction. He quarrels about the $18,000 house being too good. What does he require as a reasonable house?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is a fair question. I think somewhere in between the two would be a reasonable one. Before one house has four bathrooms every house should have one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: An $18,000 house does not usually have four bathrooms.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
According to my
information, quite a few of them have. I saw some houses built in Regina last year and I understand that they were not able to get bathtubs for many of them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do you want four?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, I do not. If we are to grant half a million dollar production subsidy to Crane's, then the taxpayers of Canada have some interest in knowing where these bathtubs are to go.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In bathrooms.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Some should go to Regina. They should not go to Forest Hill and Toronto, because the people there are able to pay, on the average, $18,000 for their houses. I suggested last year that the minister should formulate an over-all plan. He should convene a conference of people who are interested in the problem of housing on the provincial and municipal level as well as on the federal level. That conference should be called immediately. It is the minister's responsibility to make sure that subsidies are provided for all those municipalities or provinces which will go along with him in providing housing for the people in the lower income groups. No private builder, no life insurance company, no group of philanthropic people is likely to go into the construction of housing in Canada with a view to providing houses for a third of the people who are living in the lower income groups or even the middle groups. The only housing that we are likely to get under our present programme is for the people in the upper third, who have a good deal of financial security and who, in all probability, would be able to build their own houses regardless of any help from the federal authority.
Before the order in council passes, the minister should make some commitment as to whether or not in the near future he will take the responsibility for calling together a conference to try to get an agreement and work started with a view to providing housing for the people in the lower income brackets.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I like to speak about what I am sure of, and I am sure of certain things

about the wartime houses in Fort William. The committee will expect me to know something about them. Several hundred houses have been built. I visited many of them. When they were built the criticism was that, while we had these houses in the first year after the war, two years after we would be asking ourselves what was to be done with them. Many of the people who were living in these houses at the time they were doing war work now want to buy them. That is the finest argument in favour of the judgment of the minister of reconstruction in building these houses. Some of these people want to buy them and put a foundation under them. I visited over a hundred of these houses and I found only one individual who was not satisfied. He moved from a shed away out in the country. He had a large family. He said: "This house should be bigger." I said, "Yes, in the same way that your family should be bigger." But when he came to find out what his rent was as compared with rents in other places he was grateful.
I should like to say another word about the wartime houses in Fort William, and especially about the work which the contractors have done. There has not been one word of criticism. Instead of pulling to pieces the work which has been done by this department, we should at least say one or two kind words.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Courtesy is a splendid thing. If a little courtesy had been shown by the minister this afternoon I would not be on my feet at the moment. I asked him a friendly question about nails and what he was going to do about them, and he said: "Go away; do not bother me about nails." I said that I was going to bother him on the floor of the house this afternoon.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale. He covered the situation pretty thoroughly. The hon. member for Mackenzie has had a good deal to say on the situation and in many instances he was correct. I myself have visited a great many of these houses. In most cases the ones built by the minister are all right. There is a block of houses in Windsor which were built on wood blocks which do not meet with my approval at all. I also saw many houses in Vancouver and I saw quite a few houses which were built just west of the Red river. In most of these places the average returned man finds the cost of the houses too high.
The hon. member for Mackenzie was alert when he was asked a question by the minister about the cost of the houses, when he said that somewhere in between was the happy medium.

Emergency Powers
That is right. In order to purchase one of these houses, a man has to show that he has practically steady employment so that he can keep up his payments. I do not know how long the employment will continue but the payments run over a long period of time. Unless the veteran is assured of employment over the period that the payments run, he is not- in a secure position.
At the moment the whole problem is nails. For two months we have heard the hon. member for Peterborough West asking about nails, and he is right. In my town I do not think you could get twenty-five cents worth of nails. How is it possible to build eighty thousand houses if we have not the nails? The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply is still our guiding hand and we are still under war measures. Therefore I say that he has the right to instruct the companies which are making nails to increase their production and do nothing but make nails. If that were done the problem would be solved in a short time.
So far as people in the low income brackets are concerned, there are a number of people in Ottawa and in every other city in Canada who are in that position. I have been through the city of Ottawa and it is a disgrace to see where many of these people are living. We do not need to go any farther than across Wellington street to see it. These men in the low income tax brackets are working only part time, and they are certainly not going to be able to purchase homes such as many of those that are being built at the present time, and at their present cost. I would urge the minister to use his authority at once to see that the nail supply in Canada is increased one hundredfold, I would say, because if we do not have an increased supply of nails within the next month or six -weeks there is no possibility of building 80,000 homes this summer.

A year ago when I brought up the question of housing we had a rather rough time, as I recall, just before the session ended; but, despite that fact we got some results, and since that time almost everything that I said on that occasion has been verified by other members who have looked more thoroughly into the question. I remember that, when speaking on this question last year, I drew to the attention of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply some of the facts in connection with wartime housing. If I remember rightly-and I am speaking from memory now-I told the minister then that, while I had not seen any of the houses under construction, I did, a day or two before coming to Ottawa prior to the last session, visit the building plant where the Shoquist Construction Company was building parts of houses which would be transferred from there to the location, wherever it might be, where they would be required. I said that in my opinion, judging from the way the houses were being constructed, the sides and so on, they would not stand up very well under the conditions to which they would be subjected.
Today I wish to discuss some of these houses. Some time ago I put some questions on the order paper in regard to these houses and I wish to quote from the questions and answers. This was in reference to the Shoquist Construction Company of Calgary:
1. How many houses has the Shoquist Construction Company contracted to build and/or has built for the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, and/or Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation?
The answer was:
Three hundred houses for Wartime Housing Limited.
The next question was:
Where are these houses located?
The answer was, in Calgary. The third question was:

The answer was:

Then under the (b) part of the questions:

That makes about three-quarters of a million dbllars and that is a lot of money, but that is the answer. The next question was:
5.	What is the contract price for each type of house ?
I am not sure about this and I would ask the minister to explain it. The answer is:
Four-room house (asbestos shingle siding), $1,900.41.
Am I to take it that the complete house with asbestos shingle siding would be $1,900.41? Then there appears in brackets "wood siding, $1,942.41". There must be something wrong there, or I am misinterpreting it.

I have not personally visited these houses that have been constructed but I have had some communications and personal interviews in the matter. One of the first complaints I had was in regard to the agreement of sale, and I wish to read a letter that I received in this connection, with a view to soliciting some information from the minister. Later on, I shall speak of other things that I know more about because of the evidence I have. I quote from this letter:
The enclosed is a cutting of an editorial in the Journal of yesterday's date. It speaks for itself and the subject matter is one it is thought should be brought up in the House of Commons. It is certainly a one-sided agreement and the price of the houses suggests the government is emulating the tactics of Scrooge-

Yes, certainly I will, and along with it I will send the clipping which is enclosed. I should like to read that clipping so that it will appear in Hansard, because to some extent it verifies the letter I have just read:
Tenants of wartime houses would be well advised to have a lawyer approve the agreement of sale before they decide to purchase. After reading one of these documents, which set forth the terms under which the Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation will transfer one of the wartime housing dwellings to tenants, the impression is left that the crown company is taking no chances.
One clause, for instance, stipulates that, if any of the terms of the agreement are not carried out, the purchaser will give up possession "without any notice to quit and without the vendor bringing any action for ejectment,"-
I think that is true in regard to the contract. I do not have the agreement of sale before me. but I have it upstairs, and as I recall it that is one of the clauses of that agreement.
-and that the purchaser is to be "without any recourse whatever . . . either at law or in equity" against the vendor, for the recovery of any moneys paid. Further, it says that in the event of any breach of the agreement all payments already made "shall be retained by the vendor as and for liquidated damages and not as a penalty."
That, too, I think is one of the clauses in the agreement of sale, as I remember it. I read this, subject to the minister's correction, but I looked up the agreement of sale when I read this article, and that is as I recollect it.
Another clause announces that in the event of any breach "the purchaser shall forthwith become a mere trespasser upon every part of the said lands, and may be forcibly ejected therefrom by the vendor or his agents without any of them being in any way responsible for damages."	*
These clauses appear to the layman to be harsh and arbitrary. In excluding any appeal to the courts of the land, they violate one of the fundamental rights of a Canadian citizen. Although the vendor is a crown company, it cannot be allowed to set itself above the law.
To represent such a document as "between His Majesty the King in the right of Canada" is to libel the crown itself. It has been charged that the bureaucratic mind is prone to arrogate to itself supreme power and authority. This agreement of sale certainly appears to be a manifestation of such a tendency.
I believe these references to the agreement of sale are correct, because I checked them when I received the article?

I am very glad the minister brought that point in, because he has referred many times to social credit as being a kind of screwy thing, but now he acknowledges that this is a screwy contract. Had I said that, the minister would have been a little irritated, but I am glad he has placed that interpretation upon it. I do not think the minister will deny that the clauses referred to as being in the agreement of sale are there, and it seems to me quite unfair that if a veteran has put money into a house; if he has paid for a certain period of time and then, for some reason or another, misses a payment, which violates a clause in the agreement, he should be liable to be ejected without any recompense in regard to the money paid in. It seems to me that, with the economic conditions under which we are living, it would be only fair for the agreement of sale to be modified to give the veteran a little leeway, in case he should lose his position, until such time as he might become reinstated in employment and be able to carry on. The minister may say, well, the company might agree to that, that no man would be kicked' out just because he happened to fail to make one monthly payment. But that is not in the terms of the contract, and, after all, when one is dealing with matters of this kind one must confine himself to the wording of the contract. That is the thing we should complain about now.
For a few moments I should like to speak about the construction of the houses. Referring to this matter a moment ago, I mentioned that I had visited the place down by the railway tracks in Calgary where the
Emergency Powers

Shoquist Construction. Company were putting together the sides of the houses, and so on. Young fellows were working there who, in my view, did not have any practical experience. I am not saying it takes men with practical experience to nail two by fours together; I do not think that is necessary, provided that they are under proper supervision. When I was speaking of wartime houses last year the Minister of Veterans Affairs said one of the reasons those houses were so poorly constructed was that they did not have first-class workmen. That was all so much tommyrot, because you do not require every man to be a first-class workman in order to build a house properly, provided that you have proper supervision. I think the minister will agree with that.
But I want to come to this clause I read a moment ago in regard to fair wages. This was brought to my attention about a day before I came to Ottawa. One of the labour unions in Calgary telephoned and asked me to come to their office to discuss this matter of labour relations with wartime housing. At that time I pointed out to them, as I want to state to the minister now, that I had not actually visited one of these houses; and, believe me, I do not go around looking for trouble, but when trouble is brought to me I have never run away from it. That was true in connection with these veterans' houses. I never went around snooping to see what I could find out. These people came to me and asked me to see these conditions, and I went. I visited this labour organization and talked to some of the men working on these houses. I have before me an affidavit to support what I am saying. I said to these men, "This is a swell time to bring this question to me. I have not even time to go down and visit the houses, to see whether what you are saying is the truth." Then I said, "I won't do anything in this matter unless you fellows will give me an affidavit that what you are telling me is true." They did so, and I have that affidavit here in my hand.
I put the question on the order paper in regard to fair wages, because I wanted to find out whether in the contracts with these companies there was a stipulation that the men working on these buildings should receive fair and decent wages. According to the answer I received from the department, that is so; under the contract they are supposed to pay decent and proper wages. What I am going to say is in relation to the Shoquist Construc-

tion Company; as far as I could find out the Bird Construction Company, which I believe is building wartime houses in Calgary-

You are entering a complaint in the House of Commons of Canada. I assume it is a serious complaint.
