subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am saying this, that I do not think a man who lays hardwood flooring properly, if he nails it properly, and puts paper in between, can make decent wages at three cents a square foot.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is a matter of your opinion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is a matter of my opinion, yes, against the minister's opinion. He said he thought it could have been done for that, and I think he said it was ten or twelve years ago. I say that under present-day conditions I do not think a man can lay flooring, and do it properly, at that price, because it is a different matter to lay hardwood flooring from laying softwood. I do not think he can do it at three cents a foot.
I have evidence to prove this. I was talking to men who were working for another company in Calgary at the same type of work, and who were getting five cents. These men explained to me that they could make fairly good wages at five cents. But. three cents is little more than half of that, and it makes a considerable difference.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not understand why the men would take a contract, if it were not profitable. Why did they not work at $1.20 an hour with the carpenters on the job?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Because the contractor would not let the work out on an hourly basis. He let it out on a sub-contract basis, and therefore they could either take it or leave it. If the minister is sure that hardwood flooring can be laid at three cents a square foot, then what was the price in the original contract? What does the government allow for laying hardwood flooring, to the original contractor?
I may be wrong-and I admit it-but my estimate is ahout nine cents a square foot.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I made no statement. My hon. friend said it used to be the price. I do not know what the price is. But I would not think a price of three cents a square foot is prima facie evidence that it is unreasonably low; because it seems to me, prima facie, that if the men are anxious to take the work on that basis it must be more profitable than -working on an hourly basis.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The point is this; when the subcontractor is able to put that out at three cents a square foot, what did the original contractor get?
My suggestion is this-and it it merely an assumption-that I believe the original contract must have called for something around eight or nine cents a square foot. If that is so, then there is too great a spread between the
price for laying the hardwood flooring, in the original instance, and in the sublet price. You have to see how it works out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are putting up a straw man and knocking him down. You say the price was nine cents?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I know that every time a contract is sublet there is a profit made on it by the original contractor. That was proven all the way through veterans housing. In this particular instance, where I have evidence to support what I am telling the minister, in these houses in Calgary the flooring was being laid at three cents a square foot. Let me read part of it:
We the undersigned have made verbal statements to Mr. Charles E. Johnston as to quality of work being done on wartime housing by the Shoquist Construction Company Limited, Calgary, and we now make these statements under oath, and do declare that subfloors are improperly nailed, having in many cases boards with only one nail and many places none, where two nails are required. In laying hardwood floors many places have up to three boards laid [DOT]without nails in them, and some floors (hardwood) are laid without paper between.
That just means this, that when you are going to chisel on labour-and I do not mean the government in this instance; I mean the contractor-where they come to the point where they are chiseling on labour and are paying unfair wages, then you will get inefficient work.
I do not make any mistake about it; these men who are qualified carpenters are going to see to it that they do make a fair day's wages. It was pointed out to me that in some instances they would leave the job at night, and that there would be two or three rolls of paper left on the job. Then they would come back in the morning, ready to go to work-and, mind you, they were getting three cents a square foot. They said: "What would you do if, when you went back to work in the morning, there was no paper. Would you stand around a half a day, waiting for paper?" I said, "No, I would not." They said, "Neither did we. We laid- the floor, because we had to earn our money."
But the point is that the original contractor should now be responsible for this job. If this is true, and if these floors are being nailed so that three or four boards contain only one nail, where there should be three or four nails, then I say the original contractor should be compelled to take up that flooring. If the specifications call for paper between the floors, and that has not been supplied, then the original contractor should be compelled to lift the flooring and put the paper there, without any additional cost.
Emergency Powers

Mind you, it cost us $1,500,000 under veterans housing to recondition these houses, just because of such mistakes as are taking place in the contracts to which I have referred. Anyone who has had any experience in building must know that these floors will last for six months or probably a year and a half.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Unless dampness gets in.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
But when dampness
creeps in and the boards begin to dry out, then will come the squeaks and cracks in the floor, and the boards will pull up. That is when the veterans will have a complaint.
We have a logical complaint. I am pointing it out to the minister at this time, without any desire to be injurious to him, or to impede the work he is endeavouring to do. That was not my intention last year, either, when I brought this matter up before the veterans affairs committee in connection with veterans housing.
I am just pointing it out in this regard because, as was indicated in the letter, the returned men are being forced to pay high prices for these places; if so, they should be getting value for their money. And if these houses are being constructed in the manner in which I have indicated-and I do not think these men would take an oath to a false statement-then I think an investigation should be made.
If these suggestions are found to be true, then the proper place for the government to claim would be against the original contractor. I would object, and object most strenuously, if next year this House of Commons were asked to pay another million and a half dollars to replace the improper work that these contractors have done.
As I said in the beginning, I have not visited the houses personally. I made that clear to the minister. But I will also say that I am going to visit them this summer, because I want to see what they are like.
Then, in regard to paint, I have had information given me in regard to it, that the paint was being put on completely by spray guns.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In other words, my hon. friend now says that he is addressing this House of Commons in connection with houses which he has not seen; that he does not know whether these statements are true or not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I did not say that I did not know whether they were true or not.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How can you know they are true?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Because I have affidavits to support them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want to make a charge in connection with this? If so, we will certainly go in and take the paint off.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is the same kind of argument the Minister of Veterans Affairs gave me last year. I am not trying to find fault with the minister as the minister of reconstruction, I simply thought he would appreciate it if these things were pointed out to him. I assume, or I will make it as strong as to say that I do assume that the minister of reconstruction is endeavouring to build the best kind of houses he can under the circumstances. I would have thought he would1 appreciate having these matters brought to his attention.
Last year, when I brought this question before the Minister of Veterans Affairs he found, on investigation, that the things I had referred1 to were true. This year I could have brought statements and photographs of some of the veterans houses in Calgary to which I was referring and which were in worse condition than they were last year when I was talking. However I could see no use in doing that, because some repairs had already been made. Since I had been given no further complaints I let the matter drop. But I have the evidence in my office now in regard to those veterans houses.
I am pointing out these things to the minister so that he can take some precaution. He may say that there has been proper supervision, but may I say that I think the greatest defect in connection with veterans housing was the lack of proper inspection. I am inclined to think we are going to run into the same trouble in connection with wartime housing. I do not blame the minister personally for these floors being laid in the manner in which I have indicated, because I know he cannot run around and personally inspect all these buildings. He must have competent inspectors to do this job, and I think that is where the fault lies. If the work is not done properly the one who suffers is the returned man. I am sure the minister does not want that condition to exist, and neither do I. I hope the minister will look into the matter and see that proper adjustments are made.

In this instance I purpose confining myself to prices upon various government projects while we have this priorities system in effect. In my opinion, because of that system the prices are excessive. One was 18 feet, 9 inches, by 32 feet, one and a half storey with basement; the second was 24 feet by 30 feet, one storey; and the third one was 25 feet by 31 feet, 8 inches, one storey. The answer brought down in the return

I should like to confine my remarks to two paragraphs of P.C. 1609 which *have to do with priorities, namely, sections (a) and (b) of paragraph 2 of the office consolidation, which read as follows:
The priorities officer shall have power,
(a)	to prohibit, control and _ regulate the making of or dealing in construction materials;
(b)	to order or require any person owning or having power to dispose of or being in possession of or making or dealing in construction materials or having facilities for making or dealing in construction materials to make or deal in such construction materials in such manner as may be specified.
Through the medium of this order in council the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply has a wide and ample allotment of powers for his purpose. I think even he will admit that the construction of houses is a most desirable and necessary thing in Canada at the present time. I think too that it would be rather a bold person who, checking back over the minister's record as Minister of Munitions and Supply during the war, would say that the minister had been inefficient or was likely to prove inefficient in the administration of the construction of housing in Canada. It would be just as serious a charge to say that he was insincere or did not wish to go ahead with this most necessary construction. The minister's war record is an admirable one. I believe he is a respected engineer and administrator, but I wish to tell the committee that the minister is definitely on the spot now because of the fiasco that he has made of the powers which have been
Emergency Powers

allotted to him and to the officials under him in giving housing to the Canadian people. That is not a personal opinion; it is not an opinion confined to this group. I would say that it is the opinion across Canada, and I am sure that the minister himself would be the first to admit that there is some basis for that opinion.
The two sections which I read from P.C. 1609 describe all the powers that the minister needs to get on with the job. He has the details right there and it is up to him to proceed. From time to time in this house he has given us statistics which, I presume, are prepared by the admirable economic research group in the department of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, to whom I wish to pay a tribute, because they do prepare statistics in a form that I, as a layman and not a technical expert, as the minister is, can follow and understand. Unfortunately, however, one does not get all the information that one wants from the answers that are given to questions asked; for instance, the answer given by the minister to the questions asked by the hon. member for Bow River with regard to the cost of housing under certain conditions, and to the questions that I myself have asked with regard to certain items on which I wanted information. I do not blame the minister for sticking to the point of the question that is asked, but many of us are not lawyers and cannot see the implications of a question when we ask it, and we have received answers that do not give us the information we seek, though answers may be technically in accordance with the terms in which the questions are drawn up. I suggest, however, that the minister errs in not assisting us to get the information that we want.

I do not think the minister is a lawyer; I understand he is an engineer; but he has under him people who are far more clever than a lot of the lawyers I hear carrying on dissertations in this house, especially when we are pressing for necessary information which we ought to have. From time to time, both in the house and outside, the minister has made statements about the building boom in Canada, and housing progress. We are told that the rate of building exceeds anything we have ever known in the history of Canada. But in his press releases there are suggestions that are not strictly in keeping with the statements that he should make as head of his department. Here is an example. I was glad that the minister said we could now buy these houses in Regina. I fear the policy is a new one declared within the last day or two, because it was not in effect when I was home at Easter. maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 106, to incorporate Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company-Mr. Rinfret-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
At the meeting of the railway committee the other day I asked for an explanation of this bill, and I am far from satisfied that this parliament has power to pass it. In the first place, this is largely a power proposition. They do propose to construct a railway, as set out in the bill; and, mind you, I believe the gentlemen who are the proposed incorporators deserve a great deal of credit for what they have done in New Ontario. I have only a few observations to make about this bill.
The other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced that in the near future a conference would be held between representatives of this country and Newfoundland in regard to that country becoming part of Canada. In view of that fact, I think it is against public policy for us to liquidate any of our assets in that part of the country. While I appreciate what these gentlemen have done in other parts of Canada in connection with the development of our resources, still we as individuals have a public duty to perform.
The names of the incorporators are set out in the preamble. They propose to construct a railway to be known as the Quebec North Shore and Labrador railway, only part of which is to be in Canada. As you know, Mr. Chairman, a large part of the huge debt of this country was incurred in days gone by in connection with our railways. We have had overcapitalization, duplication and waste; branch lines were built all over Canada paralleling other branch lines, and private ownership made such a mess of the whole thing that a royal commission had to be appointed to recommend certain principles to be followed in future in connection with new railway construction. That was in 1917; and it was recommended that the board of railway commissioners, now know as the board of transport commissioners, should be consulted and should make recommendations before any more branch lines were constructed.
When our railways were built the companies came to the dominion government and were paid so much a mile to construct the lines. Then they were given rights of way, land, mineral rights and all that sort of thing right across Canada. Not satisfied with that, some of them went to the provinces and obtained1 further grants. For that reason, and in view of the conference to be held with Newfoundland, I believe that we should mark time until the cabinet has had a chance to look into the situation; then this bill might be brought in a little later in the session. This company proposes to construct a railway
Private Bills

from the St. Lawrence river in a northerly-direction to the southern boundary of Labrador, thence in a northerly direction to a point on the northern boundary of Labrador in the vicinity of Ruth lake, and even on the Ungava bay, Hudson strait and so on. The company is making provision to go through another country, because Labrador does not belong to Canada. Labrador was given to Newfoundland, and during the war the provisional government appointed by the British government for Newfoundland automatically looked after Labrador.
In view of the coming conference, I fail to see why we should give the terms asked in this bill. True it is that this company did apply to the Newfoundland government, and simply got permission to go on with the railway. We note the words, "provided that authority be obtained from Newfoundland." What power have the incorporators of a railway company to go to a country which is not part of Canada and negotiate, over the heads of parliament, for the building of a railway?
In addition to the railway, they are to have permission to issue securities, and other things besides. They are to have power facilities to develop. They are to be placed in control of aeronautics, something which is under the control of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), as he pointed out when the aeronautics bill was passed.	.
Then, they are to have power over certain amalgamations, and they are given power to generate, acquire, use, transmit and distribute electric and other power or energy, arising from the water power up there. That is a pretty wide departure fom the Railway Act. If it is to be a power corporation, and not a railway, why do they come under the Railway Act? Further, it is not for the general advantage of Canada, because no doubt when they come to parliament they will want a grant of so much a mile for the construction of the railway, despite the fact that it is through a first-class mining district.
Then, they will have to erect telephone andi telegraph poles, and they will require wharves for purposes of navigation on the ocean and on inland lakes and rivers. They will have the right to build docks and warehouses, and act as wharfingers. Many other things enter into this contract. They may construct, acquire, charter and navigate steam and other vessels for the conveyance of passengers, goods and merchandise; and may construct, acquire and dispose of wharves, docks, elevators, and so on.
It is an omnibus bill; they are given everything. Further, they are allowed to construct

hotels and parks, and all that kind of thing. They are given jurisdiction over motor buses and motor cars for collecting, carrying, transporting and delivering freight, goods and passengers, and may collect rates and charges therefor; but no rate or charge shall be demanded or taken until it has been approved of by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada.
Another power they are given-and I have never seen this placed in a railway bill before -is that of building a pipeline for oil, so that they may transmit via pipeline right through a country which does not belong to Canada. Why, we might as well pass a bill here to do these things in the state of New York or the state of Maine.
We do not own Labrador; we have nothing to do with it. Yet, here, over the head of the cabinet and the government, there is a proposal to go through all this, to go through an outside country, with the authority of Newfoundland. While Newfoundland is in the empire, it is still another part of it, and is now placed under British trusteeship. I should think that would be the proper way to describe it, for Great Britain lias the responsibility.
I shall .point out one further fact, and then I shall have concluded, because, having said this, I have done my duty as a member of parliament. I have attempted to look into the situation to see that we are not guilty of giving certain things in a haphazard fashion. It will be noted this bill was initiated in the other end of this building. There were no reporters at the meeting, and what was said was not put on the record. As I said in committee, "You have money to spend, to take down divorce proceedings; but you have not money to spend to report the proceedings of the railway committee, when you are giving away a franchise, and all that kind of thing." I objected to it. We should have had a record of it, so that we would know what they are asking. But somehow or another, everyone ignored it.
We might as well be handing over the whole of Labrador, a place we do not own, to a lot of private people. Do not forget the mistake that was made in New Ontario. I would suggest that we look at "Moody's Public Utilities"-"Huston's" used to be the national financial book

and see who owns the natural resources of Canada. Look over the natural resources of this country, the gold, silver, copper, nickel and other minerals, from the Ottawa river to the Nipigon, and you will find who owns it-Americans and other foreign

Private Bills
capitalists. You will see who they are; they do not live in this country at all. And they are not Canadian citizens. I object to that.
I am one who has always supported private capital, because we owe a great deal to capitalists from all over the world who helped develop this country. But if you pass this bill to enable them to obtain this franchise, they will have the power to spend money. I do not object to these men personally; they are fine citizens of Canada, and have done a great deal for Canada and themselves. They have a good record in other places. But I believe that in the public interest it would be unwise for us in this haphazard fashion under this omnibus bill, to part with natural resources we do not own in another part of the empire.
We have squandered the natural resources of this country at a great pace and Canada is going to be a poor country with its debt. To a large extent we have given away our natural resources to mostly a lot of outsiders, and some insiders. The result is that rates for power are away up to a point three times what they should be. That is about all I have to say about the matter. These are good people; but I fail to see that this bill should pass, allowing them to receive this handout for largely nothing.
Another point I wish to make is that we are committed to a 99-year lease on bases, from Newfoundland to British Guiana, between Britain and the United States. That lease was given with the consent of Canada. We have given to the United States leases on all the bases in the Atlantic ocean, including some on the shores of Newfoundland and Labrador. The bases are not all out in the ocean, because some are on Greenland, Iceland and other places in the north country, including Newfoundland and Labrador, the territory under the joint defence board and the atomic board.
This proposed agreement is ultra vires of the dominion. At the end of the bill it is brought under the Railway Act by saying that it is declared to be for the general advantage of Canada. Let me say that it is for the general advantage of the promoters; that is what it is, and not for the general advantage of Canada by any stretch of the imagination. That is so, because of the decisions in the law courts. All these properties are not even in Canada. In this bill they are being handed everything from the heaven above, the earth beneath and the waters under the earth, in Canada, Quebec, Newfoundland and Labrador.
They are being handed all this by parliament in a haphazard manner, and we have no power to do it.
That lease which was given for ninety-nine years is practically a freehold. In Washington, in congress and the senate, they are urging that Newfoundland and Labrador be given to America, although the lease for ninety-nine years was to protect United States shores in the battle of the Atlantic, and that it should be cancelled and charged up to lease-lend, because that is what it was for, to defend America's shores from invasion. When the enemy was threatening Newfoundland and Iceland, Labrador and all the Atlantic seaboard, and when they were right up the St. Lawrence we met in secret session, and the case was stated by a former able minister, who is now the premier of Nova Scotia.
For these reasons I believe the government should lay down a policy in connection with this bill. What is the government's policy regarding handing out this property? We have no power to do it, because if we go to the law courts it will be found that this is outside altogether, and not for the general advantage of Canada. We might as well put railways in Spain or Greenland, or any other part of the world, under our Railway Act, as to say that this property belongs to Canada, and it is for the general advantage of Canada. Take a look at this book, Who's Who, "Moody's Financial List of Mines and Natural Resources of the World". My hon. friends to my left used to look it up, years ago. Who owns the natural resources of this country? We had a big fight about that in Ontario from 1905 to 1914 when Sir James Whitney came into office. Our friends on the other side of the house gave the water power in the Niagara River to private owners, with the result that the rates were top heavy. The greatest mistake Sir James Whitney made was when he did not electrify the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway in 1909 or 1910, so that they could have had cheap light and power in that part of new country. Gold production, silver production-the production of all the great minerals-could have been carried on with cheap hydro power. If Ontario men had electrified the T. and N.O. railway and brought the joy of cheap light and power to the great mines of all New Ontario and cheapened prospector and development costs as Sir Adam Beck wanted to do then, it would have been then $9 or $10 a horsepower instead of having to go up as high as $35 or $60 a horse-power at Cochrane and other mining centres under private ownership.

That is something we should consider when dealing with a bill like this. As far as I am concerned, it means nothing to me and I do not care a snap of the finger further if you want to pass such a handout under this bill as I might as well rather go home, if you do.
While I appreciate that these are great Canadians, that they have done a great deal for the country as well as for themselves, still I believe it is not the time for us to part with natural resources thus. I say this because of the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that a meeting is to be held to consider a new province, Newfoundland. Newfoundland is badly enough off now with her debts because of the money that was squandered there and because of the way the natural resources were handed out. If Canada is going to pull them out of debt she will have to pay a lot of money out of her own pocket, especially with regard to Labrador. I am a member of the railway committee, and I consider it my duty as a member of the House of Commons to make that statement in the public interest and object to the bill, and having said this, that is all the objection I have to the bill.

However, that is neither here nor there. If this company goes on to develop the iron ore in this area I wish it every success. We can certainly do with a lot more iron ore in Canada and in the United States. We all know that the great Mesabi ore beds west of Duluth in the United States are being rapidly depleted, so much so that the United States government is setting aside I have read certain iron ore areas for future defence purposes. I hope there is a large bed of iron ore in Labrador and northern Quebec. We are in the iron age, and if the ore in this area is of good

quality and in a sufficient quantity it will be a grand thing for Canada. I have always been one who has advocated the opening up of the resources of this country.
The description in the bill is not clear as to whether the iron ore beds are near Grand falls on the Hamilton river.

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This section gives authority to the company to construct and operate a line of railway running into Labrador, which is not a part of Canada. I would ask the minister what is the meaning of these words: provided that authority be obtained from Newfoundland for the construction and operation of this section of the railway-
Note this:
-thence northwesterly to a suitable port on Ungava bay.
There is no port there at the present time. Will this interfere with the negotiations between Canada and Newfoundland as to the latter joining Canada, announced in the house the other day by the Secretary of State for External Affairs? And where is the port on Ungava bay? Do the words I have quoted mean that this company can negotiate with another government over the head of the government of Canada? Can a private company and private people do this? I should like to know from the Minister of Transport whether the Canadian National Railways has abandoned this territory on the St. Lawrence and in Labrador.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I will try to answer some of the questions involved in the request made by the hon. member. What is being done here has two aspects. One is the incorporation of a company which thereby gets the right to act as a person; the second is the grant to that company of the right to build a railway in Canadian territory. Under our system no one, neither a company nor an individual, can build a railway without a charter from the government of Canada if it is to be interprovincial or if it is to connect Canada with another country, or from a province if the railway is to be entirely within the province. This parliament can grant no rights to build a railway outside its territory, but it can give a company the capacity to receive such rights from the appropriate authority. That matter came before the privy council several years ago. One was a case concerning the John Deere Plow Company, and the other was a case concerning the Bonanza Creek Mining Company. The capacity to receive powers can be granted by this parliament in creating a corporation, and that is all that this parliament can do with respect to any portion of the railway that would be outside Canadian territory. It can have the capacity to receive a franchise from the sovereign of the territory outside Canada where it may operate. I do not think that would be dealing with a foreign government over the head of the Canadian government any more than it would in the case of a United States company that gets a charter here for the operation of a subsidiary in Canada. There does not appear to be any international conflict here. All states assert the right to give companies the capacity to receive powers from whosoever may be willing to grant powers to them.
With respect to the port on Ungava bay I have no information whatsoever. I do not know whether there is a port there or whether one can be developed there. But reading the bill I gather that the intention is to have a

railway that would go out of Canada, through Labrador, then come back into Canada and proceed through Canadian territory toUngava bay. But the company will not be able, under this charter, to do anything outside Canada without getting a franchise from the sovereign of the territory outside Canada where it may desire to operate.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
We are a party to Great Britain's granting of a ninety-nine year lease, binding Canada with America, which is practically a freehold of all the Newfoundland bases, and that includes Labrador inland as well as on the ocean. In view of that agreement, have we the power as a parliament to go into Newfoundland and give away, not only the bases, but the land and the bay where they are trying to develop a port? Ungava bay is a big bay and they have no port there yet, and the bill is in the dark on it. Have we the power to do this in view of the ninety-nine year lease made by the British government with the United States for the use of all these bases in Newfoundland and right down to British Guiana, which is the size of Great Britain? You know, Mr. Chairman, that in the last war German boats came right up the St. Lawrence and we had a secret meeting of parliament in connection with that. I contend that Canada is bound by that ninety-nine year lease and that we have no power to part with this property.
These people told the railway committee that they had dealt with a former Newfoundland government before the war. I would ask the Minister of Transport, what was the nature of the arrangement, if any, the said company made with the old provisional government of Newfoundland? What form did it take? Was it just an act of the provisional government? If it was, no wonder Newfoundland went bankrupt. I think the committee is entitled to this information. Does not the agreement with the United States for a ninety-nine year lease of bases include not only the bases on the ocean but the bases on the land and in Newfoundland and all of Labrador, and all the inlets on the coast? In the last war German boats were up near Iceland and Greenland, off Newfoundland, and in the St. Lawrence and Hudson strait, and we had to send ships up there. It cost a lot of money and lives.
The House of Commons is passing this bill blindly, and we shall regret it in the days to come if we hand over all this territory to private ownership forever. It is not a work for the general advantage of Canada. It is

not even within Canada. So how can it be for the general advantage of Canada when the territory and inlets are not in Canada at all? We might just as well claim that inlets and coves in China are works for the general advantage of Canada. I should like to know if the legal department of the crown has been consulted about this bill. I do not like to worry the Minister of Justice. I shall not ask him for his legal opinion, but I think he should have been consulted as to whether this bill is worth the paper it is written on. It goes over the heads of the Canadian and British governments and over the head of the provisional government of Newfoundland. Great Britain had a temporary trusteeship over the whole country of Newfoundland while the war was on. I should like to know who drafted and recommended this bill. I think all that information should be on the table. So far as I am concerned I do not think it makes any difference. I feel that I have done my duty as a member of parliament in calling the attention of the committee to what is involved in this omnibus bill.
Most of the people are fine people. They are not being criticized personally at all. I do not blame them for coming to parliament and asking for this legislation, because this is a pretty easy institution which we have assembled here. Nobody would give away that property in this way if they owned it themselves. What we are dealing with here is the mining industry.

The hon. gentleman who preceded me got mixed up in the various companies that are interested in this project. The company may lay out, construct and operate a railway.

I said that the Canadian National Railways, when they decide to build a branch line or a main line into new territory, make a survey and determine whether or not the natural resources are such, the population is such, and the revenue which may be derived from traffic is such that it will make the line a revenue producing line. I have repeated that many times and I attempted to paraphrase it quickly this evening. I may not have put it in the same words as before; to summarize the situation briefly, that is the position.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
That is a sound way of doing it. I am not arguing against what the minister said. Nevertheless, until the resources of the country are known and surveyed, it is hardly likely that population will be a factor.
I remember well working at -the time of the construction of the Canadian National Railways. I scowed on the old Fraser river from Tete Jaune Cache to what is now Prince George, and there was no population except the workers engaged in construction and the odd settlers in the Moose river area, and so on. It was the natural resources at that time that captured the attention of the Canadian National, as well as the potential earning power of the railway. This one may have an equal potentiality, and if it has, then the development of these resources will build up the population. If a private company such as this feels that its survey indicates the possibility of the undertaking being profitable, then it seems

Emergency Powers
to me that it is a proper thing for the Canadian National Railways and its owner, the Canadian people, to give careful consideration to the question whether it should not go into this development as a public enterprise, rather than leave it to private enterprise.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Cheaper for you to take them over when you are the government.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: That is a possibility; we will keep that in mind. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has given us an idea there, and we will write it down in our little black book and in a few years' time look into the question.

speechtext: Don't put it in the red book.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
That is one of the things we should not like to do, to take over a $60 million or $100 million concern that is worth only $5 million in intrinsic value.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South made a good point when he suggested that the bill should not go through but be given further study. I attended one of the meetings of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. One of the witnesses was there-I have forgotten his name-but no record was kept of the meeting, and I asked the chairman if we could not have a written brief from the promoters so that we could examine the position. We were not given that brief. Whether we shall get it I do not know, but certainly there was nothing at that meeting to suggest that we would get it, and I have heard no more about it. I think it would be a good thing to supply the members of the house with a brief from the company so that we can understand the situation exactly and know what the known resources and possibilities are. If that were done we could give the matter more intelligent consideration and come to a better decision. I believe that would be the right thing to do.

The joint defence board and the atomic bomb board have been in this territory and I think we ought to know what the policy is. They have been roaming all over the territory, all over Labrador, Newfoundland, Ungava bay and Hudson bay, but we have no report from them. There is another board there, the atomic board, from which we have received no reports. Since it is nine o'clock now, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that further consideration of the question be held over until the next occasion when the bill comes up. This is not the first time I
have come to the relief of public ownership, to protect our natural resources, and it may not be the last.

speechtext:
As I indicated before the dinner recess, the order in council that we are discussing at the moment gives the minister of reconstruction wide powers, permitting him to look after the urgent needs of the Canadian people for housing. As I intimated this afternoon, I think it is the general feeling of the Canadian people that the minister, whose record as Minister of Munitions and Supply was so brilliant, has failed dismally in doing the job that we as Canadians expect of him, and in taking such steps as would render that job easier in the exercise of those powers that parliament has delegated, as contained in this order in council with respect to the construction of large-scale housing to satisfy Canadian requirements.
I just wish to indicate again that in 1946 the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, with all the fanfare that has accompanied the various bills and amendments, with the National Housing Act, which has been on the statute books for so many years, provided less than 12,000 housing units for ownership by the occupants or for rental. That figure wjas made up of 6,927 houses for ownership, on which the corporation gave loans, and 4,836 rental houses for which the corporation lent money. I am prepared to admit, of course, that there are other agencies working in this country to provide some measure of housing; but in view of the wide powers granted the minister under P.C. 1609 I think it is fair to say he is not only a super-optimist in his statements about housing but he is optimistic beyond all reason.
The two sections I read before the dinner recess indicate the power given the minister
Emergency Powers

speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend which months those were?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

That is not an unusual situation in itself, but what was the situation in 1946? Since housing needs have not diminished, one would expect the picture to be a little different in that year. However I do not believe the minister has changed the balance between the number of houses needed and the number under construction by one solitary housing unit since he took office; I am quite convinced of that. In 1946, instead of four months during which there were more unplaced applicants than there were unfilled vacancies, the period was seven months: January, February, March, April, May, November and December. From this it would not seem that the minister has gone about his job in connection with housing with the vim and vigour with which he is credited with having undertaken Canada's war effort.
The cost of building material has gone up, as I have said, not only in connection with the kind of lumber for which I asked the minister to provide figures, but in connection with most of the other articles that go into the construction of houses. In that regard one would imagine the minister would use some incentive, other than the kind he gave Crane's recently, to increase the production of building materials, since there is going to be a demand for them for a considerable length of time.
I notice in the report to which I referred a minute ago, "Housing in Canada", we find at page 44 that the production of cement for 1946 is over that of any of the years from 1939 to 1945. The same applies to the

Emergency Powers
production of bricks, warm air furnaces, asphalt shingles and gypsum wallboard. But with respect to sawn lumber last year, despite all its requirements, there was less sawn lumber produced in Canada than in either of the years 1941 or 1942. Then, in respect of glass, which is an imported article, but which, nevertheless, I have no doubt the minister has sufficient power to do something about, in 1946 we secured less glass than we did in 1939, 1942 or 1944.
In connection with castiron soil pipe and fittings we dropped below the high record of 1941. Then, referring to steel pipe tubes and fittings, we were beaten last year by all six years from 1940 to 1945 inclusive. In wire nails and spikes, about which we have heard so much, we had the lowest record last year of any year from 1939 to 1945. Last year we produced 58-9 thousand tons, and the lowest previous year, during the war, was 1944, when we produced 64-9 thousand tons.
I should like to conclude by putting on record the approach to the housing problem in terms of a country which, I believe, does lead the world. Canada does not, despite what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply have said. I should like to set out here the Swedish housing budget for the fiscal year 1946-47.

speechtext: I am quite prepared to bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not
going to talk about veterans houses, nor am I going to talk about wartime housing. I wish merely to present the case of the small town. I think the private builder who wishes to build his own house, not for sale or rent but rather for his own occupancy, is the forgotten man in the housing programme. I have been trying to find out just where he fits in. I have been reading the minister's speech of February 7, in which he spoke about the new ruling in connection with housing. He points out rightly that we have not been able to construct as many rental units as we had hoped, and points out, further, that during 1946 seventy-five per cent of the completed residential units were built for sale. I think all will admit that most of those were built for speculative purposes.
I believe the minister is right in trying to promote the building of units for rental purposes. But in the small towns there does not seem to be any place for the priority of the man building his own house. If there is a large-scale building programme under way, and a contractor is building a group of houses for veterans or wartime housing, or on any other kind of project, there seems to be a way of getting materials. If you are building 100 houses you can get bathtubs, plumbing, flooring and finishing materials; but if you are only an individual in a small town you will find it difficult to secure materials.
I made a survey of the requirements in my constituency, and I shall set out some

Emergency Powers

of the replies I received to the questionnaire. The first one is from the town of Moosomin. The board of trade of that town states, through its secretary:
The housing situation in town is very difficult. I believe that there is need of from 30 to 50 new houses at least. If material were easily available, I am sure that there would be that many homes started almost immediately. _
And so on, right through the list, from all the towns in my constituency. Broadview is a divisional point on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway. Many hon. members will remember it. The board of trade in that town tell me that not only are they short of construction materials for the building of houses, but they lack finishing materials, plaster board, Donnaconna board, masonite, ten-test and wall boards of all kinds, casings, baseboards and flooring. One further thing of which they are in short supply is nails. However I shall not touch upon that, because someone else has already done so.
Then, at Rocanville they have no community centre, except an old hall, which is in very bad condition. They have tried to raise money for a memorial hall. I submit that this is much more important than a new cocktail bar or a new bowling alley, because they have no other place in which to hold a community gathering of any kind. But they have been held up for over a year through lack of cement and lumber.
Then, the Grenfell board of trade, through its secretary, tell me that they have not been able to honour permits to veterans to build, because they have not been able to get the lumber to fill the permits.
And right through the whole catalogue of towns in my constituency we find the same story. Some need more than others. At Indian Head, for instance, the town in my constituency where the experimental farm is located, the situation is so bad that building of any kind has practically come to a standstill. The lumber dealer at this point was able to obtain only three cars of lumber during all of 1946, and only two cars so far this year. It goes on to say:
Those connected with the building trade in the town state that at least eight cars of lumber, including two cars of flooring and finishing lumber could be immediately disposed of to private parties wishing to build their own homes.
This is one of the few towns with running water and it is only because of their hook-up with the experimental farm that they have running water. They say that plumbing supplies and sheet metal are also in very short supply and difficult to obtain and that this shortage will have to be overcome before

normal building can take place. I am not suggesting to the minister how he is going to do this, but I understand that the priorities officer has jurisdiction. I again plead with the minister to give consideration to these people who are not carrying on large construction projects which might have a claim on the basis of great volume. I am sure, when he thinks about the matter, he will realize the handicap these people face in presenting their case in connection with supplies.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am sure the committee recognized in the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Parkdale a valuable contribution to the knowledge of this committee in deliberating on P.C. 1609. I should like to offer my congratulations to my colleague upon an outstanding and' valuable contribution to this dtebate.
The order before the committee confers wide powers upon the minister, which, by a later order, were transferred to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Powers were conferred not only with respect to the distribution of construction materials but also with respect to their manufacture.
We have had reports from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply from time to time concerning the manufacture of construction materials. It is perhaps only natural that, in view of the unsatisfactory situation which exists, the attention of the committee should be directed principally to the aspect of the distribution of these materials rather than to the subject of their manufacture. Actually some improvement has been shown in the past year in the rate of manufacture of building materials, although the steel strike of last summer created a disastrous set-back to the manufacture of certain building products. Whatever may be said about the improvement-it is not a great or general improvement -in the picture with respect to the manufacture of construction materials, the picture represented with reference to the distribution of construction materials is not a bright or happy one.
It is just over a year ago that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply came into the house and sought to wash his hands of his responsibility for the channeling of construction materials into home building. On April 1, 1946, the minister announced1 that order in council P.C. 1184 had been passed on March 27, 1946. In the acompanying statement he referred to the fact that on December 5, 1945, construction control was abolished, but that subsequently a special committee from the Canadian construction association, as well as a large number of municipal and other organi-

Emergency Powers
zations, including veterans' organizations, had recommended that all types of construction other than housing be prohibited or controlled. In the face of that, the minister proceeded to announce an order in council, the effect of which was to divest himself andi the federal authority of all power of directing the use of construction materials by simply handing responsibility over to the municipal authorities.
Whatever might be said about the situation in normal times, what was done by the minister of reconstruction on that occasion was to part with the effective means of ensuring that the available supply of construction materials in Canada should be devoted to home construction. That kind of passing the buck offends the conscience of the Canadian people. Here we were with a limited and quite inadequate supply of construction materials, and the power rested in the hands of the minister to channel that supply, inadequate as it was, into home construction. But he publicly washed his hands of the problem and simply threw it over into the hands of the municipal authorities.

speechtext: Is this the same hon. gentleman who, no later than last autumn, demanded that all controls be abolished?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: For what does my hon. friend want to issue permits?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
A permit plan would have helped greatly in seeing that construction materials were channeled into home construction, and that power was available to the minister at the time. The power was available at the time to see that construction materials were denied to projects which were postpon-able or not essential, in order that all available supplies might be used in home construction. The minister did not do that and the priorities system which he set up has since proven itself quite inadequate. A permit system would have provided a means which would have been effective for this purpose, but the minis-
Emergency Powers

ter passed the buck to the municipalities. As everyone knows, a municipal body is not equipped, nor is it a proper body to deal with this problem. As everyone knows, municipalities are competing with one another to attract industries. They are not going to refuse permits to concerns which wish to come in and build. The result has been that there is no effective control by the municipal permit system. Municipal councils have not been applying any selective method to channel construction materials into the building of houses. What has been the result of this washing of the hands on the part of the minister of reconstruction and divesting himself of his responsibility in the situation? Let us look at the number of permits granted in 1945 and 1946.
In 1945 the permit system was in effect for the first eleven months of the year, and here are the figures issued by the dominion bureau of statistics and to be found in Hansard of February 17 of this year. Let us just see how the proportion of permits for home construction bulks in the total of permits issued. In 1945 permits for house construction totalled, in round figures, $117,000,000 out of a total of $197,000,000 of building permits. In other -words, about sixty per cent of the permits in terms of value were for home construction.
What happened in 1946 when we did not have the permit system? 'Permits for home -construction totalled $200,000,000 out of a total -of $383,000,000. In other words, the percentage of construction materials going into non-residential construction is growing, and that is bound to be so. Every member of this house has seen for himself the effect of allowing industrial construction and all forms of post-ponable construction, non-essential construction, to compete with housing construction for the limited supply of building materials. Let me remind the committee of what Brigadier Storms, general manager of Housing Enterprises Limited, had to say about this matter. He was dealing with this very situation and with the excuses sometimes offered on behalf of the minister that industrial construction and other forms of construction do not take the same kind of materials as residential construction and do not absorb labour of the same kind. Here is the answer to that kind of talk. This is what Brigadier Storms is quoted in the Toronto Globe and Mail of October 10 last as having said on this subject:
Bricks, cement, plumbing, electrical fixtures and other materials which should be going into housing are being used for millions of dollars' worth of non-essential building. Douglas H. Storms, general manager of Housing Enterprises of Canada Limited, asserted yesterday in an interview.
(Mr. Fleming.]
"This country has gone berserk on building of the wrong kind." he said. "Everywhere you see plant extensions, theatres, garages, stores, summer cottages, dance halls and hot-dog stands under construction. You can't tell me those buildings don't take material away from housing because they do. What is more, they are absorbing thousands of workmen who should be building houses.
"At the same time, people are living in the worst distress for lack of houses. On one street of small houses in Xew Toronto, we found that each house was occupied on the average by 19 people. All this non-essential building goes on and we cannot get houses built for homeless people."
He added with reference to the subject of control by the municipalities:
"If you can show me a municipality in Ontario which is exercising the slightest selective control over building I'll buy you a new hat," Mr. Storms exclaimed.
During the war and the ensuing control period building was restricted, he said. Once the restrictions came off business corporations and individuals, all with money to spend, had rushed in to build. Firms were now building big plant extensions which, he said, would stand empty a few years hence "when the honeymoon is over."
The honeymoon is not yet over. It is going on full blast todays. On every hand you can see people proceeding with construction that might well have waited until the imperative needs of home construction have first been met. It is a sad commentary on the record of the present government that it has to some extent been participating in the honeymoon. In the city of Ottawa we had the remodeling of the Ottawa theatre of the national film board, a government agency-, and this was done at a time when people are living under conditions such as Brigadier Storms described- nineteen people to a house, veterans living in hovels, garrets and cellars, whole families housed in a room or two. Yet the government of Canada feels free to participate in this honeymoon of building.
These are not the only unhappy, deplorable results of the way in which the government has been mishandling the control of construction materials. A black market is flourishing today. Distribution has been disarranged; the normal channels have all been upset; stock-piling has been going on, as was related this afternoon by the hon. member for Park-dale, on projects which have enjoyed favour under the present priorities system, and the private builder, /who is still expected by the government to carry- the brunt of the load, must scramble for what is left.
Last year we were told by the minister of reconstruction that there were built in Canada, through original construction or reconversion, 60.000 housing units. We have been told, in a return filed recently in the house, that a

Emergency Powers
total of 10,009 of these housing units were built under various forms of government housing, most of them under Wartime Housing, some under the Veterans' Land Act, some under integrated housing, and a very few by Housing Enterprises Limited. The number completed in 1946 by Housing Enterprises Limited was, according to a recent return, only twenty-eight housing units. Housing Enterprises Limited started off in 1946 with an objective of 6,000 housing units. In the middle of the summer that objective was dropped to 3,600, and at the end of 1946 only twenty-eight had been completed. Subtract 10,009 from 60,000 and you will find that
50,000,	or five-sixths of all the houses that were built last year in Canada were built by private enterprise builders, The government is still counting on therp to carry the load. It would be difficult, after a year has gone by since the government passed this buck to the municipalities, to resume the permit system. But the present priority system has proven quite inadequate and quite unsatisfactory. The government divested itself a year ago of the means it had at its disposal of ensuring that the available quantity of building materials was channeled into home construction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think I should say just a word in reply to the speeches we have heard this evening. The speech of the hon. member for Eglinton indicates the state of utter confusion in which the official opposition finds itself on the matter of controls. It spent six or seven weeks of this session demanding that all controls be removed, and now we have the hon. member for Eglinton insisting that new controls be put on, especially the one control which, throughout the war years, was found to be unworkable and exceptionally unfair under any administration we couldi operate. Hon. members suggest that, while cities insist on competing for new industries, they would be quite content to have the government decide that one should be built and) the other should not. It seems to hon. members quite simple for anyone to sit in Ottawa and decide what is essential. I perhaps might give an example. To my mind, the building of a plant in Saskatchewan to process horse meat would not be an urgent project, and yet I got not only a demand to grant a permit but a demand for priority assistance in doing so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You thought it was, did you not?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We granted the permit, but we did not give priority assistance. You can take as many projects as you like. What is one man's meat is another man's poison.
A great deal has been said about the scandalous waste in building bowling alleys. Yet we have had the most pathetic requests, during the period of controls, for permission to build bowling alleys in towns in northern Ontario, and elsewhere in Canada, where bowling is the one recreation of a considerable body of people in a small community.
We have looked into building control thoroughly and found that it was difficult of administration. We found that violations of the control were not punished in the area, because people in the area would say, "Nonsense; this is essential building. They can say it is not essential in Ottawa, but we know it is essential and we are not going to punish this man for violating the order." That is one of the reasons why building control was one of the first controls to be abolished. Nothing can be built in a city unless some civic body decides that it should be built in the interests of the city. Any city has the right to refuse to have anything built, and I may say that some cities have refused. For instance, the city of Kitchener have been most punctilious in choosing the type of construction that can be built in that town. The city of Regina has also cooperated in that regard. I could name other cities which have done their part to see that the material supplied to that area was channeled into housing construction.

speechtext: Did Ottawa ask for permission for the Capital brewery to put up their new building?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

That may be so. The control of priorities has been gradually relaxed, as have all controls. Starting two years ago. we had much more insistent demands than today to abolish controls and to get back to the normal law of supply and demand. It would appear that by the time we are ready to let go controls the opposition will be full out for a completely new system of controls. That is the only conclusion I can reach after listening
Emergency Powers

to their performance this evening. However we are maintaining controls on two basic commodities, lumber and steel,. and we do maintain a system of priorities for limited classes of house building; that is, buildings under government sponsorship, which includes wartime housing, integrated housing, veterans housing and Housing Enterprises Limited, the insurance company project which is supported by government finance. Furthermore we issue priorities to houses being built for individual veterans after the house is fifty per cent completed. The reason for the fifty per cent rule is to prevent the requirement for a priority for material which may be diverted into less essential types of construction. We feel that there is no great difficulty about getting the material which goes into the first fifty per cent of the building; that the need for priority really exists only in the second stage of building.
Reference has been made to the small number of houses built last year by integrated housing. The reason for that is that the plan was started only last year. A great many houses under the integrated plan were not completed at the end of the year and therefore did not appear in the 1946 figures. It is estimated that there will be at least 10.000 houses built under the integrated plan in 1947 and probably about seven or eight thousand houses under the wartime housing programme, which is about the same size as the programme of last year.
Reference has been made to the individual project in the small town. It is very difficult indeed to devise a priority system for that type of building. The builder buys at retail from the local hardware store. Of course, when material is supplied to that hardware store there is no way that we know of, of guaranteeing that it will go to housing rather than to the building of farm properties or less essential building. However we do try to see that each small town gets its fair quota of building materials. Constant study is being made to create efficient means for encouraging house building in the small town. I may say that government housing projects are available to small towns as they are available to larger towns and to cities and that no request for housing under government plan from the small town is being turned down.
The supply of building materials has been improved this year as against last year. Reference has been made to nails. The production of nails this year is the largest in recent years. They are being produced at the rate of 1,400.000 kegs, which is larger than any year since 1938.

We export no nails and have not done so for some months.
We have been asked why we cannot make more nails. The reason we cannot make more nails is that we are using all the wire that the Canadian mills can produce in a way that seems to be the wisest way to use it. When discussing one problem people are apt to forget all other problems. If we use all the wire that Canada produces in this country to make nails, there will be no wire to make agricultural implements; there will be no wire for baling purposes on the farms and no wire for a number of essential uses for wire. We have cut the supplies to these other uses down to the finest point that we believe possible and are using the remainder of the wire to make nails.

markets; but none are being exported at the moment. I do not know that I have any further points that should be mentioned. However we are trying to limit the extent of the controls as gradually as possible. We assume that hon. gentlemen do not want us to start expanding controls again. We are gradually working out of controls in an orderly way. and whenever a supply situation

Emergency Powers
becomes satisfactory the control is dropped. There are controls of two basic commodities we believe to be essential to permit industry to develop at a maximum rate, and the purpose is to continue to control steel and steel products, and to control timber until we can make the supply situation adequate in both these fields.
I said before that, through a tight control of steel, we are producing about twenty per cent more steel products in this country than would be possible without the control. We are taking excess raw products away from steel plants that have capacity for producing a greater supply of raw products than finished steel, and turning them over to other steel plants that have finishing capacity in excess of capacity to produce raw materials. We are bringing slabs and billets from Algorna into the Hamilton area; we are moving pigiron from Algorna into all foundries in Ontario and Quebec; we are moving billets from Nova Scotia into Montreal and Hamilton; we are moving pigiron from Dosco back into central Canada, a movement that was unheard of until the past year. We are using all the productive capacity of the steel mills and, by using all that capacity, we are keeping the finishing capacity of the steel mills and foundries going at full capacity, and have brought about a balance. That requires rigid control and a careful juggling of the raw materials.
As far as lumber is concerned, we find that the use of this commodity is exceeding the requirements of the last year, and we are taking orderly steps to decrease the proportion of exports of lumber and to divert greater supplies of Canadian production to the Canadian market. Further announcements will be made of progress in that direction within the next week or ten days.
It is difficult to administer controls at the present time, far more difficult than during the war years. In the first place, we have not the personnel available in peace time that was attracted to the government service during the war. We also find that people were much more amenable to instructions from government in war time than in peace time, which is quite understandable. However, such controls as we have left are reasonably effective and we believe they are amply justified by the results being obtained from them.

speechtext: I did not intend to get into the question of the merits of any of these controls, because I felt that would be more adequately handled by those who have been following these particular controls more closely than I have, but I cannot help making one or two comments on the minister's last statement when he dealt with the question of handing over to the municipalities the issuing of permits with regard to these building materials upon which priorities still exist.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I set my hon. friend right. He is about the tenth man who has said that we handed over to the municipalities the right to issue building permits. The municipalities always had the right to issue building permits; they have had it since confederation. The only thing we handed to them was the right legally to refuse building permits, and we did that as a result of a case in Toronto where the city refused a building permit. The man to whom the permit was refused took legal action and the court ordered the city to grant the permit. But to say that we handed over the granting of building permits to municipalities is ridiculous.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the minister wants to split hairs and enter into a fine argument we can go on with that for the next hour. But in effect what he did was this. Having taken to the federal government the authority to say that this or that building should be built and this or that building should not be built, he then gives back to the municipalities, if he prefers to use those words, the right of issuance. But he did not at the same time part with his priority system of controls with regard to building materials. The only point I am making here is that it is not proper; it is putting an unfair burden on the municipalities, and particularly the small municipalities, to do the one without doing the other. If the minister maintains, as he appears to, that priorities on building materials cannot yet be abandoned; if he is going to retain that measure of control, he should retain the other measure of control in order to make the whole scheme effective.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to understand my hon. friend. Is he advocating that all priority controls be dropped? Is that what he is advocating?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Then what is he talking about?

I suppose* having listened to the argument all day, consciously or unconsciously the minister may be arriving at the {Mr. Wright.]
point where he may not wish to follow it farther, but the point I am making is that if you are going to maintain control over building materials by means of priorities, as the minister is doing, then it would be logical and fair particularly to the small communities if you would retain control over building permits. I know that in the case of a municipality such as the one I come from, where a small industry-wishes to become established it can bring tremendous pressure to bear on that municipal council. They come along and say, "We wish to get a permit to construct this building". The municipal council wish to give priority to housing, and they reply, "We are sorry, but we are giving priority to houses. We are giving all our permits to those who wish to build houses and for the moment are deny-ing them to those who wish to build garages, recreational centres and other types of buildings". Then the industry comes along and say-s, "We are sorry, too; we imagine we shall have to go down the valley and put up our plant somewhere else". So that the municipality is in an almost hopeless position. If it denies that permit it may lose an opportunity- to provide employment for its residents, while if it grants the permit it means that materials which otherwise might be used for the construction of houses will be denied, for the time being, to those who wish to build homes. So I say it is placing an unfair burden on the municipalities to put them in that position. As long as it is necessary to maintain priorities in regard to building materials-and at the moment I am not entering into the merits of that case-it would have been fairer to retain control over the granting or denying of building permits, because half a measure is worse than no measure at all.
When I rose this evening I said I had not intended to enter into that part of the discussion until the minister made the remarks he did in reply to the hon. member for Eglinton. Mv purpose in rising this evening was to draw attention to those provisions of this group of orders in council which are similar to the provisions in the wartime prices and trade board order, which the Minister of Justice indicated he would be prepared to amend in the same way that the other order was amended.

The department is conferring with cities every day. I think not a week goes by when some officer of the department is not conferring with almost every city in Canada. Some cities are more cooperative than others, but all have worked with the government to a greater or lesser extent in providing housing.
The attitude of the provinces is definite. They say, "The dominion has accepted the problem, and it is the dominion's problem. Just carry on. We are not interested." I might point out that the dominion is in the housing field simply as a result of the maladjustment of population which occurred as a result of the war. It is quite out of its jurisdictional depth, and it has no business in housing. Housing is in the field of the provinces and the municipalities.
However we have entered the field, first by making ample money available for privately built housing; and, further, we have sponsored certain government plans for housing, which are being helpful. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I should like to ask the minister of reconstruction, or possibly the Minister of Justice, a question, and possibly make a suggestion. However I would be more apt to be governed in the matter by what the Minister of Justice might say.
In most of the orders in council which are being considered here, the priorities officer or the controller, as the case may be, is given power to delegate his power. This is done, for instance, in section 5 of P.C. 1609. It seems to me that the wide powers these controllers are given should not be passed around like, for instance, hot cross buns, or something like that. These are important powers; they are extensive, and extend over the freedom of the people. There should be some limitation in the delegation of such wide powers.
Would the Minister of Justice say that it is essential for the proper carrying out of the duties of the officers in question that they should have the power to delegate the extensive powers they have. If this delegation of power is necessary, then I suggest to the Minister of Justice that the people to whom the powers can be given should be limited.
Another point I would raise, while I am on my feet, is one which arises under section 12 (2) of P.C. 3, at page 141. Perhaps it is because we do not like to see the ordinary freedoms which have been set up for years affected or infringed upon, but it does seem to me that a controller should not have the power he is given in that subsection. Where a controller believes that any person has failed to produce books and records, under this subsection he can authorize in writing a police officer, police constable or other person to go in and make seizure of the books. Such officer may enter by force, if necessary, and carry those books, not to a court, or to a place where they would be in the custody of the law, but he shall carry them before such controller.
It seems to me that, in 'the first place, the controller should have no licence whatsoever to give a warrant or order under his hand to authorize a police officer to enter the premises of a person. In the second place, if that power is necessary, and is given to such controller, any records seized should be placed in
