I should like to give the committee two or three of the prices that were quoted to me over the week-end. I understand that the ceiling price in Canada for gyproc lath is $30 per
1.000	feet; it was offered to me at $47.75 per
1.000	feet. I understand that the Canadian ceiling on metal lath is forty cents a yard; it was offered to me at fifty-four cents a yard. I was offered cement at $1.25 a bag and nails at $20 to $25 a keg. I was informed that the supply was abundant and that I could get materials at those prices.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I suggest to my hon. friend that he try dealing with somebody on the other side of politics and he m;ght get the right prices.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is pretty cheap.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am dealing with two contractors, but unfortunately I have not inquired into their politics. All I wanted to know was whether they could build a house. Here we have an apparent abundant supply of building materials, abundant at what they call the imported price. It is reported to me that these building materials have been imported from the United States, but I do not know whether that is so because I have not examined into it personally. I am simply taking the word of my contractor, who is a large contractor and knows what he is doing.
This is the story I get not only from my own people but from other contractors throughout the district ; they can get the material but they have to pay these extra prices. The building industry tells me that these extra prices are the result of the priorities system imposed on the building trades by the government. In other words, they say that if the Canadian building material industry were allowed to ration or sell on a completely open market without having to meet certain government priority commitments, the prices the average man is now asked to pay would not be charged because there would be a greater supply of building materials. There are many hundreds of houses being built. Not only do they take four or five months longer to build than they should under normal circumstances, but some take even a year longer, and I am told by the same builders quoted by the member for Parkdale this afternoon that that is entirely because they cannot get building materials since they are held up by the priority system imposed bjr the present government.
[Mr. Adamaon.l
I do not want to quote my own case and I do so merely because I happen to have specific information. I know, because I am interested in the building business, exactly what people are up against in the city of Toronto todaj'. Material is simply not available unless the builder or the owner is prepared to pay extortionate prices. Perhaps these prices that have been quoted to me are the proper prices to pay. But then why go through the fantasy that control and a priority system do exist? Why not free the whole thing and let the building industry do its own rationing of materials? Here we have hundreds of houses in a semi-finished state, over sixty per cent finished. They may or may not be finished this summer because of the inability to get materials. When you have a house under construction the time element is infinitely more important in many ways from the point of view of cost than any other. When you have a gang working and they are held up for two or three days waiting for materials the cost of labour soon goes up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If you have to wait for materials it is because you are building so many factories in your riding.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think that is the reason at all. It is true that industrial development has been great, as it has been throughout Canada. As was stated this afternoon, the industrial development is several times the domestic house development in dollar value. If, as the government says, the main problem is the building of dwelling houses, why does it allow industrial construction to exceed domestic construction by several times? That was one of the problems which was discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Parkdale.
But my point is not the question of industrial development versus domestic housing. My point is this. How is it that material can be obtained at these excessive prices or above the ceiling prices and cannot be obtained at the ordinary prices? Either the government by its policy has thrown a monkey wrench into the production of building materials, or something in the economic system is very wrong, and I suggest through you, Mr. Chairman, to the government that serious consideration and study be given to this business of producing building material. Either the building material industry in Canada cannot produce the building materials required, or the government by its action is stultif3'ing the production and distribution of building materials. Building materials are simply not available for private building.

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member who has just taken his seat has just mentioned lath and sheeting. I have a memo here from the Department of National Revenue regarding export permits. I notice that export control was imposed on gypsum wall board, lath and sheeting on April 3. How much of it was shipped out before that date?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I could not say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: After export control comes in, the permits issued before that date still run for another six months. Is the minister allowing these permits on building material to run for an extra six months? On nails, export control was imposed on February 2, 1946, but the permits which had been issued before that date were allowed to run for a further six months. The minister suggested that the hon. member try to deal with other people besides those of his own party. On March 31 the hon. member for Middlesex East asked a question regarding nails and I said a couple of words on the subject. I was out in the hall here a few minutes after and was offered ten kegs of nails at $14 a keg, and I refused. The man who offered me them was not of our party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That happened in this building?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have the figures here on nails for 1946. They show that we exported 25,410 hundredweight, practically all to Newfoundland and the British West Indies. We imported in the same period 13,605 hundredweight, chiefly from the United States. I would say that that is a very tight control, having in mind our historic obligation to look after the West Indies.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That was wire nails. You also exported iron nails to the amount of about $500,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: After listening to the minister and others taking part in this debate, I am more convinced than ever that if we are to provide homes for the Canadian people controls of building construction must be not only maintained but extended. I note, under "Powers of Priorities Officer", that he has power to order any person in possession of or dealing in construction materials or having facilities for making or dealing in construction materials to make or deal in such materials in such manner as may be specified. I would suggest that in this respect, "in such manner as may be specified", more restriction should be applied. I think most members of the house and most right-thinking Canadian citizens will agree that the production of homes for Canadians is an urgent matter, and particularly so because so many young veterans are looking for homes. We do not have to go very far afield to find them. I think it is much more important to provide for the construction of homes than for the construction of theatres, despite what the minister said tonight. It is much more important to provide houses for our people than to provide theatres, bowling alleys, hot-dog stands, breweries and luxury hotels such as are being built in Montreal at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where are they being built?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You do not have to go very far. I was there the other night and I saw it. There is a lot of building material in that one hotel which, if spread around, would provide houses for hundreds of veterans.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is housing also.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If there is insufficient building material to meet the demands for house construction it is quite unfair to permit the building of structures such as I have named. Furthermore it is a bit unfair to place the onus upon the municipalities to decide what type of construction should be permitted. The reason is that there may be areas in Canada where the housing situation may not be as serious as in others. In such cases the municipal authorities may feel quite justified in authorizing the construction of buildings which would use up the available supplies of materials. That is why the federal authorities are the ones best able to assess the situation throughout the country and the only authorities able to channel the material into the type of construction that is most needed. It is the governing body which should exercise that control. Restriction should definitely be placed at this time on non-essential building if we are to provide the houses that are so badly needed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
A few moments ago the hon. member for York West made a serious statement, particularly with the Minister of Justice listening. The hon. member for York West said quite definitely that there is a black market in building materials operating in Ontario. He also said that the contractor with whom he is dealing in the purchase of lumber knows where to secure lumber on the black market. If that is true it should be investigated by the government. I am not sure whether it is true. I have another opinion on it. I know there is a shortage of materials across Canada. The minister will remember
Emergency Powers

that I wired him last November about eight veterans houses which were tied up for some months because of lack of certain materials. The contractor was a veteran. He could not get materials. These houses were standing for months. Across the street from him another contractor who was building luxury houses had all kinds of material. There was no difficulty, but the veteran contractor told me that the reason for that was that those who were building the luxury houses were paying black market prices. At that time I tried to find out who operated the black market, where the material came from and so forth. I did not succeed in running it down. If the hon. member for York West knows who is operating that market in Ontario, or his contractor knows, it should be checked up.
Perhaps something else is happening. We may find out that all our weeping about material shortages may be caused by a holdup. There may be a hold-up by manufacturers and lumber dealers in Canada to make building materials unavailable, for the purpose of breaking price ceilings. If there is lumber available for a black market that lumber is in Canada and should be on the market. That lumber can come only from legitimate *dealers in this country and they know where it is. If it is held up for a squeeze in order do break price ceilings so that they may get *whatever price they want for the lumber, the chances are, if the ceilings are taken off, you will not be able to buy that material, the cost would be so high.
As regards this fellow that we are crying about, the veteran and the chap who wants to build low-priced houses and the contractors who want to build low-priced houses for rental, which today they may be able to build under the ceilings for S3,000 or $4,000, similar houses will cost $10,000 with the ceilings off. If that takes place the fellow who is making lumber available on the black market will be able to charge whatever price he wishes. On the other hand, if you remove controls altogether the chances are there will be no lumber in Canada at all if they will pay higher prices for it in the United States, in South Africa or in some other countries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he know of any place today where you can build a house for three or four thousand dollars? I have been trying to find one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I know of a number of places. The first determining factor is the kind of house you want.
[Mr. Gaiis.J

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: He wants a luxury house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In Kamloops?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can take the hon. member to a section of the country that is quite a distance away from here and show him many cooperative housing projects that were set up under a provincial government act where you can get a seven-roomed house with a good basement, complete radiation, all modern conveniences for $1,800.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I mean today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Today that same house could be built for about $2,500.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is it being built?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A contractor would not build it. A private enterprise contractor would charge about $6,000 for the same house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can you build them for that today?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the thing we are trying to avoid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The question I asked the hon. member was, can you get them built today for three or four thousand dollars?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I said that under the same scheme, the cooperative housing groups, you can build them for about $2,500.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Today?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Certainly you can, but, as I said, you would be eliminating free enterprise. That would be the people working for themselves. Under these circumstances I do not think the hon. member would ever get a home.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Or a carpenter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
What I am trying to find out, Mr. Chairman, is whether the accusation made by the hon. member for York West is correct or not. If it is not correct I am suggesting that perhaps the minister should probe the field of where lumber is available at certain inflated prices and find out whether the private enterpriser and lumber dealers in this country are putting on the squeeze in the building of houses. I feel sorry for the minister in this matter of housing. It is pretty bad in the end of the country from which I come. Perhaps lumber is in shorter supply in that part of the country than in any other part of Canada.

Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are lucky if you can get them built for three or four thousand dollars.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I said, under certain circumstances. A moment ago I said that lumber is short there. I realize that in the maritime provinces, if it were not for the control of lumber, there would be no lumber in that part of the country. At least we are getting some kind of quota, because there are some regulations on it. I suggest that in this matter of controlling lumber and maintaining ceilings in this country the government should carefully consider the proposition from our free enterprise friends. They all have good houses. They are not worrying. This crying on your shoulder about veterans not having homes and all that sort of thing is so much bunkum.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are just as much interested in the veterans as you are.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We are not so much interested in veterans' politics as the hon. member is.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They have not fooled me for one minute. I have seen these salty tears and I have seen section 98 passed and all that kind of thing the minute they got in power.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have done much more for veterans than you have.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I remind the committee that it is almost eleven o'clock. There is an order in council before the committee for consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Could I wind up some amendments tonight?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am about through, but I intend to follow this up, because an investigation is due on the part of the government into the accusations made tonight by the hon. member for West York. If there is a black market and he knows where it is operating it is up to the government to find out, and if a black market is not functioning, then it is a disgrace to break the price ceilings. Where is this lumber coming from which is available for a black market? It is produced by the legitimate industry of the country and it must be coming from there. If it is coming from there, then there is a squeeze to smash the price ceiling and get back to free enterprise.	,

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The department takes great interest in low-cost housing for people of small means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
When the people of
Canada agreed to price controls with regard to
building materials they were under the impression that the government itself would carrj' out a housing programme to provide houses at the lowest possible figure. In my particular section of the country, if I may be permitted a personal reference, Wartime Housing started operating in the city of Yorkton and in September, 1945, there was a contract for the construction of ninety houses, but after eighteen months there are still about twenty-five of these houses to be finished. The people are told that it is a matter of supplies of materials. During the winter there was a small fire in which the contractor lost some material. At any rate, these are not low-cost houses; because some six-roomed houses cost up to $5,000, and they are built without basements. After eighteen months there are still many houses not ready, and veterans in my constituency have been living in trailers all winter. Some people told me that one had to go to a contractor on the other side of politics. That is a rotten state of affairs. The people of Canada expected that government controls would provide houses, hut we still find that there are those who cannot get houses, though materials are available for building hotels and similar structures. Hotels in the city of Montreal have been mentioned. That sort of building does not go down very well with people who cannot get homes. They are looking to the government for action, because it is the government's responsibility, and when the people do not get action they feel peeved about it, particularly when they find that contractors can get materials for building theatres and the other kind of buildings that are being put up. What does the government intend to do? Does it intend to tighten up, or is it going to throw the whole thing over the wall?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How long has that contract been going? It sounds as if there should be a change of contractor.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The contracts were signed in September, 1945.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: For 125 houses?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No; ninety.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And how many have been built?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They have moved into sixty-five now, I believe. That was the situation at Easter when I vras at home. The rest are not yet occupied.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Why did the Saskatchewan government not build them instead of making boxes?
Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I move:
That the following be inserted in the schedule to the act in the column entitled "Amendments" so as to pertain to order in council P.C. 1609 of 23 April. 1946, as amended:

Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shall the order in council carry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What about section 5 in the same order in council, with reference to delegation of powers? I think the minister should consider an amendment to that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We cannot consider an amendment to that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Will the government give a reason? I cannot see why the great powers given to the controller should be delegated without even designating to whom they are delegated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: One man cannot give decisions from coast to coast. He must delegate power to outside officers. That has been necessary over a period of several years, and we could not operate without it for the rest of the time the order operates. The office would be meaningless if we did.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Could not the minister at least limit the people to whom these powers may be delegated? Could they not be limited to responsible senior officers, instead of being made applicable to "any person or persons"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I move, Mr. Chairman, that the following be inserted in the schedule to the act in the column entitled "Amendments"-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Portage la Prairie asked a question and he should receive an answer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We cannot operate without the power to delegate. That is self-evident. It does not require an elaborate debate at this stage of the evening. It has always been in the act. The power to regulate involves the power to delegate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I point out that this is a very wide power.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is a power we have always had.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It says that the priorities officer shall have power to delegate from time to time, to any person or persons, any power vested in the priorities officer under these regulations, including any power involving the exercise of a discretion, and any' order made 
in the exercise by any such person of a power so delegated shall be final and binding unless and until it has been varied or vacated by the priorities officer. The hon. member for Portage la Prairie has asked if it would not be possible to restrict to senior officers the group of people to whom the power might be delegated. The way it is worded, the power could be delegated to any employee at all, and that is going much too far.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Even for a Tory.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What officer would my hon. friend suggest? Would he want to select them?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The minister has mentioned that there will have to be officers in different parts of the country. I can see the need for delegating powers to the man in charge in Vancouver or in Halifax. Why not say that? Why is it necessary to take power and delegate it to the newest clerk? The minister does not contend that a wide power of that sort is necessary.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: My hon. friend realizes that the controller has responsibility' as well as authority, and he must exercise both. I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite would attempt to lay down rules for the exercise of his responsibility.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: This is power of a sort that should not be put in any legislation passed in this house or in any other house in the British empire. We have no objection to having the order in council go through tonight, but I would ask that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply' and the Minister of Justice over the week-end see if there cannot be some more definite description of the officers to whom that power is to be given.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can assure my' hon. friend that care is exercised by all concerned before power is delegated to any officer; we make sure the officer is capable of administering that power. That statement is supported by the fact that since 1941, when many of these powers came into existence, committees of this House of Commons have examined the work of these controllers, and they have never brought to light any misconduct on the part of anyone to whom power has been delegated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Some fif the officers under these different boards, administering these controls in Winnipeg and other cities, have a great idea of power. I do not think some of them ever had any' power before, and that is the type of people to whom I do not believe such power should be delegated. If that is the

Emergency Powers
type to which it is going to continue to be delegated, then I shall not cease to object every time I possibly can rise in my place. When you delegate these powers to people who have never had responsible jobs before, they certainly exercise them. I do not consider it fair that the rights and almost the freedom of the people of this country should be dealt with in such loose fashion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext: I rise to a question of privilege.
